body.text:
Vinītadevakṛtā Santānāntarasiddhiṭīkā
[mūlasahitā]
body.translated_text: <s>Vinītadeva</s>'s Commentary on the Proof of Other Mental Continuums (<s>Santānāntarasiddhiṭīkā</s>) [with the root text]

children.translated_text: Having seen an action preceded by thought in one's own body, from the apprehension of that elsewhere,
if the intellect cognizes [another] mind—even in the [position of] mind-only, this reasoning is the same.
He who, the Teacher of the World, declared 'All this is mind-only'—
having bowed to him, for whom the existence of other mental continuums is established, [this] is examined.

body.text: buddhipūrvāṃ kriyām ityādiślokenāsya prakaraṇasyābhidheyasambandhaprayojanāni darśitāni / tatra santānāntarasattābhidheyam / santānāntarasattāyāḥ siddhiḥ prayojanam / tasya prayojanasyāpi prakaraṇenānena sādhyamānatvāttena sahāsyopāyopeyalakṣaṇasambandhaḥ / kāryakāraṇādisambandhānāmasminnevāntarbhāvānna pṛthagvacanam / bāhyārthavādinaḥ kila vijñānamātratāyāṃ santānāntarasattā nopapadyata iti codayanti / tathāhi, ta evamāhuḥ - yeṣāṃ cittamātrameva sat, asaṃśca bāhyārthaḥ, na teṣāṃ prāṇyantarapratipattaye pratyakṣapramāṇamasti; jñānamātrasya svāṃśamātrālambanatvāt, vastutastu ālambanābhāvāt / nāpyanumānam, kāyavākkarmābhāvāt / atha kāyavāgvijñaptibhyāṃ prāṇyantaramanumīyate cet; vijñānamātratāpakṣe kāyavākkarmaṇorvijñaptī na staḥ /
body.translated_text: By the verse beginning 'having seen an action preceded by thought,' the subject matter, connection, and purpose of this treatise are shown. Therein, the subject matter is the existence of other mental continuums. The purpose is the proof of the existence of other mental continuums. Since that purpose too is to be established by this treatise, its connection with it has the character of means and end. Since the connections of cause-and-effect and the like are included within this very [connection], they need not be stated separately. The proponents of external objects (<s>bāhyārthavādins</s>) raise the objection that in the [position of] mere consciousness (<s>vijñānamātratā</s>), the existence of other mental continuums is not tenable. For they say thus: 'For those for whom consciousness alone is real and external objects are unreal, there is no direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) as a means of valid knowledge for cognizing other beings; since mere consciousness apprehends only its own aspect, and in reality there is no [external] object of apprehension. Nor is there inference (<s>anumāna</s>), since there are no bodily and verbal actions. If one infers other beings from bodily and verbal expressions (<s>vijñapti</s>)—in the position of consciousness-only, bodily and verbal actions as expressions do not exist.'

body.text: nāpyāgamaḥ sambhavati, tasya rūpaskandhāntarbhāvāt, etasya ca pratikṣepāt / tathāhi, āgamaḥ śabdātmako vā bhaved vyañjanasvabhāvo vā / ubhayamapyetad bhavatpakṣe nāsti / nāpi tadviṣaye rūpiṇa āgamasya prāmāṇyamiṣyate / yato hyayaṃ viṣayaḥ pramāṇadvayaviṣayātīto mataḥ / tathā sati, āgamādapi prāṇyantaraṃ pratipattuṃ na śakyata iti cet?
body.translated_text: 'Nor is scripture (<s>āgama</s>) possible, since it is included within the aggregate of form (<s>rūpaskandha</s>), and this [aggregate] is rejected. For scripture would be either of the nature of sound or of the nature of phonemes. Neither of these exists in your position. Nor is the validity of scripture, being a material entity, accepted regarding this subject. Since this subject is considered to be beyond the scope of the two [other] means of valid knowledge. This being so, even from scripture, other beings cannot be cognized'—thus they object.

body.text: tathā vipratipannā bāhyārthāvādina evaṃ vaktavyāḥ / vayamapi pratyakṣataḥ prāṇyantaraṃ naiva pratipadyāmahe / na hi pratyakṣādarvāgdarśinaḥ prāṇyantaramavagacchanti / nāpyāgamo vyañjanasvabhāvaḥ / kintu praṇetṛvaśād yo vākyapadavyañjanaviśeṣapratibhāsijñānotpādaḥ saḥ / sa tu pratipattṛsantāne sannapyupacāratastathāgatasya vā kapilasya vā kaṇādasya vā karturvacanamiti vyapadiśyate / evaṃ sarve 'pi bauddhā vācakaṃ śabdasāmānyākāraṃ jñānaṃ manyante; na cāsti śabdaviśeṣaḥ, 'tasya pūrvamadṛṣṭatvād' ityādihetubhiḥ viśeṣākārasya vācakatvabhāvapratiṣedhāt / vayamapi nāgamataḥ prāṇyantarapratipattimabhyupagacchāmaḥ, api tvanumānāt / taccānumānaṃ kāyavākkarmaṇorabhāve 'pi yathā pravartate yaddarśayitumāha - buddhipūrvāmityādi / eṣa tāvat samudāyārthaḥ /
body.translated_text: The proponents of external objects who are thus confused should be told: 'We too do not cognize other beings through direct perception. For those of limited vision do not apprehend other beings through direct perception. Nor is scripture of the nature of phonemes. Rather, it is the arising of a cognition in which particular phonemes of sentences and words appear, due to the author's intention. That [cognition], though existing in the cognizer's own mental continuum, is figuratively designated as the words of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, or of <s>Kapila</s>, or of <s>Kaṇāda</s>, as the author.' Thus all Buddhists consider the cognition having the aspect of a general sound-form to be the signifier; and there is no particular sound, since by reasons such as 'it has not been previously seen,' the capacity of a particular aspect to signify is denied. We too do not accept the cognition of other beings from scripture; rather, [we accept it] from inference. And how that inference operates even in the absence of bodily and verbal actions—to show this, [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] says: 'having seen an action preceded by thought' and so forth. This, then, is the overall meaning.

body.text: avayavārthastūcyate / buddhiḥ jñānam / sā cātra gamanāgamanasaṃlāpecchārūpā parigṛhyate, kriyāhetutvāt tasyāḥ / sāsti pūrvaṃ yasyāḥ kriyāyāḥ sā buddhipūrvā / pūrveti śabdenātra kāraṇasya nirdeśaḥ, kāraṇasya pūrvavartitvāt / yadi nāma bāhyārthavādibhiḥ svasantāne tāṃ buddhipūrvāṃ kriyāṃ pratyakṣānumānābhyāmupalabhya paścātparasantāne grahād vivakṣitarūpā dhīḥ vijñānaṃ gamyate, tadā cittamātre 'pyeṣa nayaḥ samaḥ / atra kriyetyupalakṣaṇam / mukhakāntiraktimādīnāmapi cittāntarasya gamakatvāt / yadīti vacanena vakṣyamāṇabidhinā parapakṣe 'numānābhāvaṃ darśayati // 1 //
body.translated_text: The meaning of the parts is now stated. 'Thought' (<s>buddhi</s>) means knowledge. Here it is taken as having the form of intention to go, to come, or to converse, since that is the cause of action. An action that has [thought] as its antecedent is 'preceded by thought.' The word 'antecedent' here designates the cause, since the cause is prior. If the proponents of external objects, having apprehended in their own continuum that action preceded by thought through perception and inference, then from [its] apprehension in another's continuum, the intellect in the intended form—the cognition, the consciousness—is understood, then even in the [position of] mind-only, this reasoning is the same. Here, 'action' is illustrative; since facial radiance, blushing, and the like also indicate another mind. By the word 'if,' he indicates the absence of inference in the opponent's position, through the method that will be stated.

body.text: anumānamabhyupagamya tulyatāṃ khyāpayannāha -
body.translated_text: Having accepted inference, he states the equality:

body.text: ātmani cittaspandanapūrvau kriyābhilāpau dṛṣṭvānyatra tayordarśanād yadi spandanamanumīyeta, cittamātre 'pyeṣa nayaḥ samaḥ / ataścittamātratāvādī api paracittamanumātuṃ śaknoti / ātmanītyādi / cittasya spandanaṃ cittaspandanam / atra spandaneti śabdaścikīrṣāyāṃ vartate / kriyābhilāpau tu kāyavāgvijñaptyoḥ / tenāyamartho bhavati - ātmani jigamiṣāvivakṣāpūrvayoḥ kriyābhilāpayordarśanāt parasantāne 'pi tau kriyābhilāpau copalabhya cittaspandanamanumīyata iti cet? cittamātratāvāde 'pyeṣa nayaḥ samaḥ / tathā sati, so 'pi paracittamanumīyāt / atra spandanetyaviśeṣeṇoktam, tathāpi pūrvaṃ cittaspandanamiti prakṛtenābhisambandhanīyam / tasmāt sāmānyaśabdā api prakaraṇasāmarthyād viśeṣeṣvavatiṣṭhante // 2 //
body.translated_text: Having seen in oneself action and speech preceded by the impulse of mind, if from seeing those elsewhere one infers the [mental] impulse—even in the [position of] mind-only, this reasoning is the same. Therefore, even the proponent of consciousness-only can infer other minds. 'In oneself' and so forth. The impulse of mind is 'mind-impulse.' Here the word 'impulse' refers to volition. 'Action and speech' refer to bodily and verbal expressions (<s>vijñapti</s>). Thus the meaning is: from seeing in oneself action and speech preceded by the desire to go and the desire to speak, if upon perceiving those action and speech in another's continuum too, the mental impulse is inferred—then in the consciousness-only position too, this reasoning is the same. This being so, he too can infer other minds. Here, 'impulse' is stated without qualification; nevertheless, it should be connected with the context: 'mind-impulse' as stated before. Therefore, even general terms become restricted to particulars by the force of context.

body.text: nanu bāhyārthavāde tu paracittanimittake kāyavākkarmaṇī liṅgatvena svīkriyete, antarjñeyavāde tayorabhāvāt kathaṃ sāmyamiti cet? evamāha -
body.translated_text: Now, [the objection]: in the position of external objects, bodily and verbal actions caused by other minds are accepted as logical marks (<s>liṅga</s>); in the position of internal objects, since those do not exist, how can there be equality? To this he replies:

body.text: tacca kāyavāgvijñaptipratibhāsi jñānaṃ jñānāntaraspandanaviśeṣeṇa vinā bhavatītyevaṃ na matam / taccetyādi / antarjñeyavādināpi kāyavāgvijñāptipratibhāsi kāyavāgvijñaptakārakaṃ jñānaṃ paracittasya spandanaviśeṣeṇa vinā bhavatīti na manyate / svajñānādanyad yajjñānaṃ tat jñānāntaram / tatsamprayuktaṃ spandanaṃ jñānāntaraspandanam, tasya viśeṣastena / viśeṣeti vacanena cikīrṣā, vivakṣā ca parigṛhyete // 3 //
body.translated_text: And it is not held that the cognition appearing as bodily and verbal expression arises without a particular impulse of another mind. 'And it' and so forth. Even the proponent of internal objects does not consider that the cognition having the appearance of bodily and verbal expression—the cognition that produces bodily and verbal expression—arises without a particular impulse of another mind. 'Other mind' means a mind different from one's own. The impulse associated with that is 'the impulse of another mind'; its particular [form is meant] by 'particular.' By the word 'particular,' volition and desire to speak are included.

body.text: bāhyārthavādimatamāśaṅkyate -
body.translated_text: The position of the proponents of external objects is raised as an objection:

body.text: atha parajñānasya kriyāyā anupalambhāt paradhīranumātuṃ na yujyata iti cet? na; tulyatvāt / atha parajñānasya kriyāyetyādi / na bhavatā kadāpi parajñānapūrvake kriyāvāgākārake jñāne upalabhyete / bhavatā tatkathamanumīyeta iti pūrvapākṣāśaṅkā / antarjñeyavādyāha - na; tulyatvāditi / naiṣa doṣaḥ / yato hi, eṣa upālambho bhavatāmapi tulyaḥ // 4 //
body.translated_text: 'Since the action of another's mind is not apprehended, it is not possible to infer another's mind'—if so objected? No, because it is equal. 'Since [the action] of another's mind, the action' and so forth. You [the externalist] have never perceived a cognition that has the appearance of action and speech preceded by another's mind. How then would you infer it?—this is the objection of the prior position. The proponent of internal objects responds: 'No, because it is equal.' This is no fault. For this objection applies equally to you too.

body.text: tattulyatvaṃ darśayati -
body.translated_text: He shows that equality:

body.text: paro 'pi parajñānapūrvau tau kadāpi na paśyati / ataḥ tenāpi tanna jñāyate / paro 'pītyādi / bāhyārthavādyapi paracittaspandanapūrvakau tau kriyābhilāpau na kadāpi paśyati / tasmāt tenāpi paracittaṃ na pratipadyate / atyantāsambaddho hyeṣa upālambhaḥ / na hi samarthanāya prasiddhasambandho 'nvekṣaṇīyaḥ, api tu doṣasāmyādeva paro nigṛhītaḥ / tasmānna doṣāntaramucyate // 5 //
body.translated_text: The other [i.e., the externalist] too never sees those two [action and speech] preceded by another's mind. Therefore, by him too, that [other mind] is not cognized. 'The other too' and so forth. The proponent of external objects too never sees action and speech preceded by an impulse of another's mind. Therefore, by him too, another's mind is not cognized. This objection is entirely irrelevant. For it is not necessary to search for a well-known connection for the sake of justification; rather, the opponent is refuted simply by the equality of the fault. Therefore, no further fault is stated.

body.text: atrāsti paracittānumānopāya iti bāhyārthavādimatamāśaṅkayāha -
body.translated_text: Raising as an objection the position of the externalists that there is a means of inferring other minds:

body.text: ātmanaścittasya paravartinornimittatvānupapatteḥ paracittaṃ jñāyata it cet? kiṃ na yujyate? ātmanaścittasya paravartinorityādi / yasmādātmanaścittaṃ santānāntaravartinoḥ kriyābhilāpayoḥ kāraṇatvena na yujyate, tasmātparacittamanumīyata iti pūrvapakṣāśaṅkā / siddhantabādyāha - kiṃ na yujyata it / kathamātmanaścittaṃ paravartinornimittitvena nopapadyate? ucyatām // 6 //
body.translated_text: 'Since one's own mind cannot be the cause of [actions] occurring in another, other minds are cognized'—if so objected? Why is it not tenable? 'Of one's own mind, occurring in another' and so forth. Since one's own mind is not tenable as the cause of action and speech occurring in another's continuum, therefore other minds are inferred—this is the objection of the prior position. The proponent of the established position responds: 'Why is it not tenable?' How is one's own mind not tenable as the cause of those occurring in another? Let it be stated.

body.text: paro 'yuktatvaṃ darśayitumāha -
body.translated_text: The opponent attempts to show the non-tenability:

body.text: svasamutthāpakacittasya pratisaṃvedanābhāvāt / svasamutthāpakacittasya pratisaṃvedanābhāvāditi / parasantānabartinau kriyābhilāpau ātmacittanimittakau vā syātām, paracittanimittakau veti dvidhā parīkṣā / na tāvadātmacittaminittakau, yasmānna svasantāne tayorsamutthāpakacoittasya saṃvedanaṃ bhavati // 7 //
body.translated_text: Because there is no self-awareness of the mind that produces them in one's own [continuum]. 'Because there is no self-awareness of the mind that produces them in one's own [continuum]'—thus. Action and speech occurring in another's continuum are either caused by one's own mind or by another's mind—this is the twofold examination. They are not caused by one's own mind, because there is no awareness in one's own continuum of the mind that produces those two.

body.text: hetupasaṃharannāha -
body.translated_text: Drawing together the reason, he says:

body.text: ātmacittaśrayiṇoścātmani darśanāt / ātmacittaśrayiṇoścetyādi / ahaṃ gacchāmi, ahaṃ vadāmīti ye svacittanimittake kāravākkarmaṇī te svasantāne upalabhyete / ātmanaścittamāśrayata iti vigrahaḥ / atra āśrayīti śabdo nimittake // 8 //
body.translated_text: And because those dependent on one's own mind are seen in oneself. 'And those dependent on one's own mind' and so forth. 'I go,' 'I speak'—those bodily and verbal actions caused by one's own mind are perceived in one's own continuum. 'Depends on one's own mind' is the analysis. Here the word 'depends on' refers to 'is caused by.'

body.text: bhavatvātmacittanimittakayoḥ svasantāne darśanam / tena kim? tasmādāha -
body.translated_text: Granted that those caused by one's own mind are seen in one's own continuum. What of it? Therefore he says:

body.text: tāvapi yadi yathā syātāṃ tādṛśāvupalabhyeyātām / tāvapītyādi / paravartikriyābhilāpāvapi yadyātmacittaśrayiṇau syātām, tadā tāvapi ātmani dṛśyeyātām // 9 //
body.translated_text: If those two were likewise [caused by one's own mind], they would be perceived as such. 'Those two also' and so forth. If action and speech occurring in another were also dependent on one's own mind, then those two also would be seen in oneself.

body.text: atha tau kathaṃ dṛśyete? āha -
body.translated_text: Now, how are those two seen? He says:

body.text: anyathā darśanādanyannimittaṃ sidhyatīti cet? anyathetyādi / ayaṃ gacchati, ayaṃ vadatītyevaṃ vicchinnadeśe dṛśyete / svacittanimittakatvābhāve sati sāmārthyāccittāntaraṃ sidhyatīti pūrvapakṣāśaṅkā // 10 //
body.translated_text: Objection: If it is argued that from perception of something different, a different cause is established? [The verse says] 'anyathā' and so forth. 'This one walks, this one speaks' — thus they are perceived in a spatially discontinuous location. In the absence of being caused by one's own mind, through inferential capacity another mind is established — this is the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (opponent's objection). [Verse 10]

body.text: siddhāntavādyāha -
body.translated_text: The <s>siddhāntavādin</s> (proponent) says —

body.text: aparasminnapi samānameva, svasamutthāpakacittasya saṃvedanābhāvāt / aparasminnapītyādi / antarjñeyavāde 'pi svasantāne vicchinnadeśapratibhāsinoḥ kriyābhilāpapratibhāsijñānayoḥ samutthāpakacittasya pratisaṃvedanaṃ na bhavati // 11 //
body.translated_text: The same applies to the other case as well, because there is no direct awareness of the mind that produces one's own [actions]. [The verse says] 'aparasminnapi' and so forth. Even according to the internalist position, in one's own mind-stream, the mind that produces the cognitions manifesting as actions and speech appearing in spatially discontinuous locations is not directly perceived. [Verse 11]

body.text: hetorupasaṃhāro 'pi tukya iti darśayannāha -
body.translated_text: Showing that the application of the reason is also equal, he says —

body.text: svacittaspandananimittake vijñāptipratibhāsinī jñāne cāntarmukhapratibhāsinī pratīteḥ bahirmukhapratibhāsinī anyanimittāditpadyete / svacittaspandananimittake vijñāptipratibhāsinī jñāne cetyādi / ye svacittaspandananimittake kriyāvākpratibhāsinī jñāne te cāntarmukhapratibhāsinī 'ahaṃ gacchami, ahaṃ vadāmi' ityātmasambaddhavijñaptipratibhāsinī pratīyete / parasantānavartinī tu 'ayaṃ gacchami, ayaṃ vadati' iti bahirmukhapratibhāsinī pratīyete / tasmādanyanimittadutpadyeta iti siddham / svacittasya spandanaṃ svacittaspandanam, tannimittaṃ yasyeti vigrahaḥ // 12 //
body.translated_text: In a cognition caused by one's own mental impulse that manifests representations, the one manifesting as inward-facing is apprehended, while the one manifesting as outward-facing arises from another cause. [The verse says] 'svacittaspandananimittake vijñāptipratibhāsinī jñāne ca' and so forth. Those cognitions manifesting as actions and speech that are caused by the impulse of one's own mind, they manifest as inward-facing — 'I walk, I speak' — they are perceived as representations connected with oneself. But those pertaining to another's mind-stream — 'this one walks, this one speaks' — they are perceived as outward-facing. Therefore, it is established that they arise from another cause. The compound analysis: the impulse of one's own mind is 'own-mind-impulse'; that which has this as its cause is the compound. [Verse 12]

body.text: bāhyārthavādī bahirmukhajñānayoḥ spandanakāraṇatve sandihati -
body.translated_text: The <s>bāhyārthavādin</s> (external realist) doubts the causal role of impulse in outward-facing cognitions —

body.text: animitte eva bahirmukhapratibhāsinīti kinneṣyete cet?
body.translated_text: Objection: Why not hold that outward-facing manifestations are simply without a [mental impulse] cause?

body.text: animitte eva bahirmukhapratibhāsinītyādi / ye bahirmukhapratibhāsinī jñāne te 'nimitte iti kinneṣyete? na spandananimittale iti vākyaśeṣaḥ / bahirmukhetiśabdo vicchinnālambane / bahirmukhaṃ pratibhāsituṃ śīlaṃ yayoste bahirmukhapratibhāsinī / nāsti nimittamanayoriti animitte / bhavatu kila nimittāmātrasya pratiṣedhaḥ tathāpi prakaraṇavaśāt spandanamātrasya pratiṣedho draṣṭavyaḥ // 13 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'animitte eva bahirmukhapratibhāsinī' and so forth. Those cognitions that manifest as outward-facing — why not accept that they are without cause? The implied completion is: not caused by mental impulse. 'Outward-facing' refers to those whose object is spatially discontinuous. Those whose nature is to manifest outward-facingly — those are outward-facing manifestations. Those having no cause — those are 'without cause.' Granted, let this be a denial of any cause whatsoever; even so, from the context, it should be understood as a denial of impulse alone as cause. [Verse 13]

body.text: siddhāntavādyāha -
body.translated_text: The <s>siddhāntavādin</s> (proponent) says —

body.text: animittatve sarvasyānimittatvaṃ prasajyeta / animittatva ityādi / yadi vicchinnapratibhāsinī kriyāvāgākārake jñāne spandanābhāve 'pi vinā kiṃcana kriyāvāgākāraṃ bhavet, tadā sarvāṇyapi kriyāvāgākārakāṇi jñānāni spandanena vinā bhaveyuḥ; viśeṣābhāvādityabhiprāyaḥ // 14 //
body.translated_text: If they were causeless, then everything would be causeless. [The verse says] 'animittatve' and so forth. If in cognitions having the form of actions and speech that manifest as spatially discontinuous, even without impulse, the form of action and speech were to arise without anything [causing it], then all cognitions having the form of actions and speech would also occur without impulse — because there is no distinguishing feature. This is the intent. [Verse 14]

body.text: tatra yadyevaṃ vicintyeta -
body.translated_text: If one were to consider thus —

body.text: vicchinnāvicchinnakṛto bhedastvastyeva / tena vicchinnapratibhāsinoḥ animittatvam, itarayostu sanimittatvamiti / ata āha - vicchinnāvicchinnapratibhāsakṛto bhedo na jñānayoḥ spandanatvanimittabhedavibhāgakṛt / vicchinnavicchinnapratibhāsetyādi / vicchinnaḥ pratibhāso vicchinnapratibhāsaḥ / tena kṛto bhedo viśeṣalakṣaṇaḥ / sa tu yato na jñānayoḥ spandanatvanimittasya bhedakaḥ; bahirmukhapratibhāsinī spandananimittake na bhavataḥ, itare tu spandananimittake iti / vibhāgastvatra vibhajya sthāpanaṃ nikṣepo vā // 15 //
body.translated_text: But there does exist a difference based on the discontinuous and continuous distinction. Therefore, those manifesting as discontinuous are without cause, while the others are with cause — to this he says: The difference based on discontinuous and continuous manifestation does not create a division regarding whether impulse is the cause of the two cognitions. [The verse says] 'vicchinnāvicchinna-pratibhāsa' and so forth. A discontinuous manifestation is one whose appearance is discontinuous. The difference created by that is a distinguishing characteristic. But that does not make a differentiation regarding whether impulse is the cause of the two cognitions — namely, that outward-facing manifestations are not caused by impulse, while the others are caused by impulse. 'Division' here means the act of distinguishing and establishing, or placement. [Verse 15]

body.text: atha nimittatvabhedābhāve ko doṣaḥ syāt? āha -
body.translated_text: What fault would there be if there is no difference regarding causality? He says —

body.text: tenāvicchinnapratibhāsinorapyanimittatvaṃ bhavet, viśeṣābhāvāt / tenāvicchinnetyādi / yato hyatra bhinnabhūtayoḥ jñānayoḥ kriyāvākpratibhāsatve na kaścid viśeṣo 'sti / tasmād viśeṣābhāvādubhayamapi spandanatvanimittakaṃ na bhavet, atha vobhayamapi spandananimittakam // 16 //
body.translated_text: Then even those manifesting as continuous would be without cause, because there is no distinguishing feature. [The verse says] 'tenāvicchinna' and so forth. Since between these two different cognitions there is no difference at all in having the manifestation of actions and speech, therefore, due to the absence of a distinguishing feature, both would not be caused by mental impulse — or alternatively, both would be caused by mental impulse. [Verse 16]

body.text: tadevaṃ jñānadvayasya sāmyaṃ sādhayitvopasaṃharannāha -
body.translated_text: Having thus established the equality of the two cognitions, he concludes —

body.text: tathā sati, avicchinnatvaviśiṣṭaḥ pratibhāsabheda eva spandanapūrvako na bhavati / kintarhi? vicchinnasyāpi kriyāviśeṣasya pratibhāsa eva /
body.translated_text: That being so, the difference in manifestation characterized by continuity is simply not preceded by impulse. Rather, even the manifestation of spatially discontinuous specific actions is just that [i.e., caused by impulse].

body.text: tathā sati, avicchinnatvaviśiṣṭaḥ pratibhāsabheda ityādi / yasmādevaṃ jñānadvayasya sāmyam, tasmād yo 'vicchinnatvaviśiṣṭaḥ kriyāvākpratibhāsaḥ sa kevalaṃ spandananimittako na bhavati / kintarhi? vicchinnapratibhāsasyāpi kriyāviśeṣasya pratibhāsamātraṃ spandananimittakam / vicchinno viśeṣo 'syāstīti padvigrahaḥ / kriyāviśeṣetyanena kriyābhilāpau darśayati / eveti śabdo mātrārthe draṣṭavyaḥ / tenātrāyaṃ samudāyārthaḥ - vicchinnāvicchinnabhedamanapekṣya sāmānyena kriyābhilāpayoḥ pratibhāsamātraṃ spandananimittakam / yato hi kaścid vicchinno 'pi pratibhāsa spandanapūrvako dṛśyate, kaścittavavicchinno 'pi nātmaspandanapūrvaka iti // 17 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'tathā sati, avicchinnatvaviśiṣṭaḥ pratibhāsabheda' and so forth. Since the two cognitions are thus equal, the manifestation of actions and speech characterized by continuity is not exclusively caused by mental impulse. Rather, the mere manifestation of spatially discontinuous specific actions is also caused by mental impulse. The compound analysis: that which has a discontinuous distinguishing feature — this is the analysis. By 'specific action' he indicates actions and speech. The word 'eva' should be understood in the sense of 'mere.' Therefore the combined meaning here is: Without regard to the difference of discontinuous and continuous, in general the mere manifestation of actions and speech is caused by mental impulse. For some discontinuous manifestation is seen to be preceded by impulse, and some continuous manifestation is not preceded by one's own impulse. [Verse 17]

body.text: tasyaiva hetorvyabhicāraṃ vyājena darśayati -
body.translated_text: He shows the deviation of that very reason by an indirect method —

body.text: śaropalaprakṣepaṇayantranirmāṇaparapracālanādikriyāviśeṣapratibhāsināṃ vicchinnasyāpi pratibhāsasya spandanapūrvakatvāt /
body.translated_text: Because even of the manifestation of spatially discontinuous specific actions such as the hurling of arrows and stones, the construction of machines, and the setting of others in motion, there is precedence by impulse.

body.text: śaropalaprakṣepaṇetayādi / śarāścopalāśca śaropalam, śaropalau ca / tayoḥ śaropalayoḥ prakṣepaṇamiti vigrahaḥ / śaropalaprakṣepaṇāni yantraṃ ca nirmāṇaṃ ca parapracālanaṃ cetivigrahaḥ / ādiśabdena māyādīnāṃ saṃgrahaḥ / teṣāṃ kriyāviśeṣastu yathāyogaṃ deśāntaragamanādilakṣaṇaḥ / tatra upalayantrayoḥ kriyāviśeṣo deśāntaragamanalakṣaṇaḥ / nirmāṇasya kriyāviśeṣaḥ kṛtyābhidhānalakṣaṇaḥ / parapracālanasya kriyāviśeṣaḥ gatilakṣaṇaḥ / yeṣāṃ jñānānāṃ śaraprakṣepaṇādikriyāviśeṣapratibhāso 'sti tāni tathā / bhavatu eteṣāṃ kriyāviśeṣāṇāṃ vicchinnaḥ pratibhāsaḥ, tathāpi spandanapūrvakatvam / etaduktaṃ bhavati - vicchinnapratibhāso 'spandanapūrvakatvena na vyāpta iti // 18 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'śaropalaprakṣepaṇa' and so forth. Arrows and stones are 'arrow-stone'; the hurling of those arrows and stones — this is the compound analysis. Arrow-stone hurling, machines, construction, setting others in motion — this is the compound. By the word 'etc.' (ādi), magical illusions and such are included. The specific actions of these are characterized by movement to another location and so forth, as appropriate. Of stones and machines, the specific action is characterized by movement to another location. Of construction, the specific action is characterized by performing and naming. Of setting others in motion, the specific action is characterized by locomotion. Those cognitions that have the manifestation of specific actions like arrow-hurling — they are thus described. Granted, the manifestation of these specific actions is discontinuous; nonetheless, they are preceded by impulse. This is what is said: a discontinuous manifestation is not pervaded by the absence of precedence by impulse. [Verse 18]

body.text: avicchinnapratibhāse 'pi vyabhicāraṃ darśayannāha -
body.translated_text: Showing the deviation also in the case of continuous manifestation, he says —

body.text: parakṛtacālanādīnāṃ cāvicchinnasyāpyatadpūrvakatvāt / parakṛtacālanādīnāṃ cāvicchinnasyāpītyādi / pareṇa kṛtaṃ cālanamiti samāsaḥ / ādiśabdena bhrāmaṇādīnāṃ saṃgrahaḥ / parakṛtacālanādināmavicchinnapratibhāsānāṃ nātmaspandanapūrvakatvaṃ dṛśyate / etaduktaṃ bhavati - bhavantu ete svadehasambaddhāḥ, tathāpi nātmaspandanapūrvakā iti // 19 //
body.translated_text: And of movements caused by others and so forth, even that which is continuous is not preceded by that [one's own impulse]. [The verse says] 'parakṛtacālanādīnāṃ cāvicchinnasyāpi' and so forth. Movement made by another — this is the compound. By the word 'etc.' (ādi), spinning and such are included. The continuous manifestations of movements caused by others and so forth are not seen to be preceded by one's own mental impulse. This is what is said: granted, these are connected with one's own body; nonetheless, they are not preceded by one's own impulse. [Verse 19]

body.text: tadevamubhayatrāpi vyabhicārasadbhāvaṃ sādhayitvopasaṃharannāha -
body.translated_text: Having thus established the existence of deviation in both cases, he concludes —

body.text: tena hyatra kriyāviśeṣamātreṇa spandanasya pratītiriti yujyate / tena hyatra kriyāviśeṣamātreṇetyādi / yasmādevamubhayatra vyabhicārasadbhāvaḥ sādhitaḥ, tasmāt kriyāvākyapratibhāsamātreṇa paracittamanumātuṃ śakyate; na tu vicchinnāvicchinnapratibhāsamātreṇa / kriyāviśeṣeti śabdaḥ kāyavāgjñiptipratibhāsaṃ darśayati / mātreti śabdo vicchinnāvicchinnayoḥ bhedaṃ nirākaroti // 20 //
body.translated_text: Therefore, it is fitting that through the mere specific action, the impulse is inferred. [The verse says] 'tena hyatra kriyāviśeṣamātreṇa' and so forth. Since the existence of deviation has been established in both cases, therefore another mind can be inferred through the mere manifestation of actions and speech, but not through the mere distinction of discontinuous and continuous manifestation. The word 'specific action' indicates the manifestation of bodily and verbal cognition. The word 'mere' removes the difference between discontinuous and continuous. [Verse 20]

body.text: tatra yadyevaṃ cintyeta -
body.translated_text: If one were to consider thus —

body.text: śaraprakṣepaṇādikriyāviśeṣāṇāṃ pratibhāsāstu vicchinnapratibhāsatve 'pi spandanatvapūrvakāḥ; tadanyā vicchinnapratibhāsāstu na tathā syuḥ? tasmādāha - tatra yadi kasyacidapūrvakatvam, na ko 'pi tatpūrvaka syāt; viśeṣābhāvāt / tatra yadi kasyacidapūrvakatvamityādi / yadi vicchinnāvicchinnajñānayoranyatarat spandanatvanibandhanaṃ neṣyate, tadā kimapi spandanatvapūrvakaṃ na syāt / kathamiti cet? āha - viśeṣābhāvāditi / sugamametad // 21 ////
body.translated_text: The manifestations of specific actions like arrow-hurling, even though having discontinuous manifestation, are preceded by impulse; but other discontinuous manifestations might not be so? Therefore he says: If any one of them is without precedence, then none would be preceded by that [impulse], because there is no distinguishing feature. [The verse says] 'tatra yadi kasyacidapūrvakatvam' and so forth. If one does not accept that either of the discontinuous and continuous cognitions is grounded in impulse, then nothing would be preceded by impulse. How so? He says: because there is no distinguishing feature. This is easily understood. [Verse 21]

body.text: upasaṃharannāha -
body.translated_text: Concluding, he says —

body.text: ataḥ kriyāviśeṣasāmānyaṃ spandanaviśeṣasāmānyasya gamakam /
body.translated_text: Therefore, the general characteristic of specific action is the indicator of the general characteristic of specific impulse.

body.text: ataḥ kriyāviśeṣasāmānyamityādi / yato hi yadi kasyacidatatpūrvakatvaṃ bhavet sarvasyātatpūrvakatvaṃ prasajyeta / ataḥ kriyāviśeṣamutsṛjya kriyāviśeṣasāmānyena spandanaviśeṣasāmānyamanumīyate / kriyāviśeṣetivacanaṃ kriyābhilāpau darśayati / sāmānyamiti śabdaḥ bahirantarmukhakṛtaṃ bhedaṃ pariharati / na hyevaṃ śakyate 'numātum - ṃrāgād vadatīti vā dveṣādvā mohādvā / tasmādeṣo 'tra samudāyārthaḥ - kriyābhilāpamātreṇa spandanamātramanumeyam, na tu spandanaviśeṣam; viśeṣe liṅgasya vyabhiucāraditi // 22 //
body.translated_text: Therefore, "by the generality of the particular action" and so forth. Since if there were non-precededness-by-that for anyone, then non-precededness-by-that would follow for everyone. Therefore, abandoning the particular action, by the generality of the particular action, the generality of the particular vibration is inferred. The expression "particular action" indicates action and speech. The word "generality" excludes the distinction produced by [the mind's being] directed outward or inward. For one cannot infer thus: 'He speaks from desire' or 'from aversion' or 'from delusion.' Therefore the collective meaning here is: by the mere action-and-speech, only the mere vibration is to be inferred, but not the particular vibration; because in the case of the particular, there would be deviation of the logical mark. || 22 ||

body.text: bāhyārthavādena samānatāṃ darśayitumāha -
body.translated_text: To show the similarity with the external-object position, he says:

body.text: tatra yathā kriyāmupalabhya, ātmani spandanānupalambhādanyatra spandapratītiḥ; tathā kriyāpratibhāsopalambhane 'pi /
body.translated_text: "There, just as by apprehending the action, because of the non-apprehension of vibration in oneself, the awareness of vibration arises elsewhere; so too when apprehending the appearance of action."

body.text: tatra yathā kriyāmupalabhyetyādi / bāhyārthavādinā yadi kriyāmupalabhya, ātmani spandanānupalambhāt sāmarthyādanyatra spandanamanumīyata iti cet / antarjñeyavāde 'pi tattulyam; kriyāpratibhāsamupalabhya, ātmani spandanānupalambhāt sāmarthyādanyatra spandanamanumīyate // 23 //
body.translated_text: "There, just as by apprehending the action" and so forth. If the external-object proponent says: 'Having apprehended the action, because of the non-apprehension of vibration in oneself, by force [of inference] vibration is inferred elsewhere' — then the same applies in the internal-object position: having apprehended the appearance of action, because of the non-apprehension of vibration in oneself, by force [of inference] vibration is inferred elsewhere. || 23 ||

body.text: bāhyārthavādinā vicchinnapratibhāsasyānimittakatvaṃ yatpūrva coditam, tadapi samānamiti darśayitum āha -
body.translated_text: To show that the objection previously raised by the external-object proponent — that the interrupted appearance is without cause — is also the same, he says:

body.text: samānametat; paro 'pi parakriyābhilāpayornimittaṃ nāstīti kinnecchati?
body.translated_text: "This is the same; does the other also not accept that there is no cause for the action and speech of others?"

body.text: samānametadityādi / bāhyārthavādyapi prāṇyantarasaṃbaddhapratibhāsinau kriyābhilāpau animittakāviti necchati // 24 //
body.translated_text: "This is the same" and so forth. The external-object proponent also does not accept that the action and speech appearing as connected with another being are without cause. || 24 ||

body.text: bāhyārthavādyanimittau nābhyupagacchati / tadavaśyamabhyupagantavyamiti darśayitumāha - tenāvaśyaṃ tau spandananimittakatvāttadabhāve na bhavata iti vaktavyam /
body.translated_text: To show that the external-object proponent does not accept them as causeless, and that this must necessarily be accepted, he says: "Therefore, it must necessarily be said that because those two are caused by vibration, in the absence of that, they do not occur."

body.text: tenāvaśyamityādi / tathāvipratipannena bāhyārthavādināvaśyamiyamupapattirvaktavyā - tayoḥ kriyābhilāpayoḥ spandanajanyarūpatvāt spandanābhāve tau na bhavata iti // 25 //
body.translated_text: "Therefore, necessarily" and so forth. By the external-object proponent who does not disagree [on this point], this justification must necessarily be stated: because those two — action and speech — are of the nature of being produced by vibration, in the absence of vibration, they do not occur. || 25 ||

body.text: athābhyupagatāpīyamupapattiḥ kiṃ tayeti cet? āha -
body.translated_text: "But even if this justification is accepted, what of it?" To this he says:

body.text: paro 'pi tayoḥ pratibhāsau tathaiva vadet / ataḥ nānayoḥ parasparaṃ bhedaḥ /
body.translated_text: "The other also would state the appearances of those two in the same way. Therefore there is no difference between these two [positions]."

body.text: paro 'pi tayoḥ pratibhāsau tathaivetyādi / antarjñeyavādyapi tathaiva vadet - vicchinnapratibhāsijñāne spandanajanyarūpatvāttadabhāve na bhavata iti / tathā sati nānayoḥ bāhyārthavādāntarjñeyavādayoḥ parasparaṃ bhedo 'sti / etaduktaṃ bhavati - yathā bāhyārthavādī parasambaddhakriyābhilāpau spandanajanyarūpatvāt tadabhāve na bhavata iti vadati, tathaivāntarjñeyavādyapi bāhirmukhapratibhāsijñāne spandanajanyatvāt tadabhāve na bhavata iti vadet / tathā sati nānayoḥ parasparaṃ kaścidbhedo / 'stīti // 26 //
body.translated_text: "The other also would state the appearances of those two in the same way" and so forth. The internal-object proponent also would state the same — that cognition with the appearance of interrupted [series], being of the nature of being produced by vibration, does not occur in the absence of that. This being so, there is no difference between these two — the external-object position and the internal-object position. This is what is said: just as the external-object proponent says that the action and speech connected with another, being of the nature of being produced by vibration, do not occur in its absence, so too the internal-object proponent would say that cognition with the appearance directed outward, being produced by vibration, does not occur in its absence. This being so, there is no difference between these two. || 26 ||

body.text: bāhyārthavādināmāśaṅkāmudbhāvayitumāha -
body.translated_text: To raise the objection of the external-object proponents, he says:

body.text: yadi tatra pratibhāsinyoḥ spandananimittakatvamucyate, svapnāvasthāyāmapi kinnocyate?
body.translated_text: "If causedness by vibration is asserted for those two appearances, why is it not also asserted in the dream state?"

body.text: yadi tatra pratibhāsinyorityādi / kriyābhilāpapratibhāsijñānayoḥ spandananimittakatvaṃ vadan yogācāraḥ svapnāvasthāyāmapi tayoḥ spandananimittakatvaṃ kinna vadatīti pūrvapakṣāśaṅkā // 27 //
body.translated_text: "If causedness by vibration for those two appearances" and so forth. The <s>Yogācāra</s>, asserting that the two cognitions appearing as action and speech are caused by vibration — the objection of the opponent [asks] why he does not also assert their causedness by vibration in the dream state. || 27 ||

body.text: siddhāntavādyāha -
body.translated_text: The proponent of the established view says:

body.text: sarvaṃ samānam / paro 'pi svapnopalabdhaparakriyāvācau spandananimittike iti kinna vadati?
body.translated_text: "Everything is the same. Does the other also not say that the action and speech of others apprehended in dreams are caused by vibration?"

body.text: sarvaṃ samānamityādi / na kevalaṃ pūrvaṃ samānam / kiṃ tarhi? etadapi pūrveṇa saha sarvaṃ samānamiti śeṣaḥ / tāmeva samānatāṃ darśayitumāha - paro 'pi svapnopalabdhaparakriyāvācāvityādi / bāhyārthavādyapi svapnāvasthāyāṃ yau parasambaddhau kriyābhilāpāvupalabhyete tau paracittanimittakāviti kinna vadati // 28 //
body.translated_text: "Everything is the same" and so forth. Not only was the previous [objection] the same. What then? This too, together with the previous, is all the same — this is the completion. To show that very sameness, he says: "Does the other also not say that the action and speech of others apprehended in dreams" and so forth. Does the external-object proponent also not say that the action and speech apprehended in the dream state as connected with others are caused by other minds? || 28 ||

body.text: bāhyārthavādīnāmuttaramāśaṅkyāha -
body.translated_text: Anticipating the reply of the external-object proponents, he says:

body.text: tayorabhāvāditi cet?
body.translated_text: "Because of their absence?"

body.text: tayorabhāvāditi cediti / svapne tu kriyābhilāpāveva na staḥ / tatkathamabhāvasya spandananimittakatā bhavedityucyet // 29 //
body.translated_text: "Because of their absence" — in dreams, action and speech simply do not exist. So how could there be causedness by vibration of what is absent? This is the objection. || 29 ||

body.text: antarjñeyavādyāha -
body.translated_text: The internal-object proponent says:

body.text: tathopalabdhisāmyāt kinna staḥ?
body.translated_text: "Because of the similarity of apprehension in that case, why do they not exist?"

body.text: tathopalabdhisāmyāt kinna staḥ iti / yathā jāgradavasthāyāṃ kriyābhilāpayorupalabdhiḥ tathā svapnāvasthāyāmapi / tasmāt kriyābhilāpayorupalabdhasāmyāt kasmānna tau staḥ // 30 //
body.translated_text: "Because of the similarity of apprehension in that case, why do they not exist?" — Just as there is apprehension of action and speech in the waking state, so too in the dream state. Therefore, because of the similarity of apprehension of action and speech, why should they not exist? || 30 ||

body.text: bāhyārthavādīnāṃ matamāśaṅkyāha -
body.translated_text: Anticipating the view of the external-object proponents, he says:

body.text: atha middhenopahatatvāt puruṣasyārthaśūnyaṃ vijñānaṃ jāyata iti cet /
body.translated_text: "But because the person is impaired by sleep, cognition devoid of objects arises?"

body.text: atha middhenetyādi / puruṣasya middhenopahatatvāt bhrāntirbhavati / tasmādarthaśūnye vijñāne jāyete / tena svapne tayorabhāva iti pūrvapakṣāśaṅkā // 31 //
body.translated_text: "But because of sleep" and so forth. Because the person is impaired by sleep, delusion occurs. Therefore cognition devoid of objects arises. Hence the absence of those two in dreams — this is the objection of the opponent. || 31 ||

body.text: siddhāntavādyāha -
body.translated_text: The proponent of the established view says:

body.text: paramate 'pi tasmādeva parādhipatyaśūnyaṃ vijñānamupajāyate /
body.translated_text: "In the other's view also, for that very reason, cognition devoid of the influence of others arises."

body.text: paramata ityādi / antarjñeyavādīnāṃ mate 'pitasmāt middhena bhrāntatvādeva parādhipatyarahite kriyābhilāpākāreke jñāne jāyete itīṣṭam // 32 //
body.translated_text: "In the other's view" and so forth. In the view of the internal-object proponents also, for that very reason — because of being deluded by sleep — cognition arises having the form of action-and-speech but lacking the influence of others; this is accepted. || 32 ||

body.text: evaṃ tāvat sautrāntikena saha samānatāṃ pratipādya vaibhāṣikamatāśaṅkyāha -
body.translated_text: Having thus established the similarity with the <s>Sautrāntika</s>, anticipating the <s>Vaibhāṣika</s> view, he says:

body.text: atha svapne 'pi jñānasyārthavattvāttadopalabhyamānānyapi santānāntarāṇyeva iti cet /
body.translated_text: "But because even in dreams cognition has objects, the other mind-streams that are apprehended [in dreams] are real?"

body.text: atha svapne 'pi jñānasyārthavattvādityādi / svapne 'pi jñānasyārthavattvāt svapnāvasthāyāṃ yeṣāṃ prāṇināmupalabdhirbhavati te ca sattvāḥ santyeva satyataḥ / tasmāt kathaṃ sāmyamiti pūrvapakṣāśaṅkā // 33 //
body.translated_text: "But because even in dreams cognition has objects" and so forth. Because even in dreams cognition has objects, the beings whose apprehension occurs in the dream state — those beings truly exist. Therefore, how can there be similarity? This is the objection of the opponent. || 33 ||

body.text: siddhāntavādyāha -
body.translated_text: The proponent of the established view says:

body.text: paraṃ prativigrahītuṃ yadi yuktyāgamarahitastathāvidho 'sadvādaḥ samāśriyeta, tadā parābhimataṃ tasya parādhipatyaṃ na ko 'pi nivārayet /
body.translated_text: "If, to refute the opponent, such an unwholesome position devoid of reasoning and scripture were resorted to, then no one could prevent the influence of others as maintained by the opponent."

body.text: paraṃ prativigrahītuṃ yadi yuktvāgamarahita ityādi / yaḥ yuktyā āgamācca rahitaḥ sa yuktyāgamarahitaḥ / yuktyāgamarahito 'sau vādo 'sādhutvādasadevādaḥ / yadi vaibhāṣikāḥ yogācārān prativigrahītuṃ tamabhyupagaccheyuḥ, anena ca mama parājaya iti / na, ayuktatvāt / tadā yogācārabhimataṃ sattvasya tathāvidhaparadhipatyamapi na kaścinnivārayet / tathāhi, bhavadbhiḥ svapnāvasthāyāṃ ye sattvāḥ abhyupagatāḥ, teṣāmevādhipatyādasmākaṃ vijñaptipratibhāsāḥ jāyanta iti vaktavyaṃ bhavet / tena hi yad viṣamatvaṃ yuktyāgamarahitatvaṃ tadevaṃ draṣṭavyam / na kutaścidāgamataḥ svapnadṛṣṭarūpasya sadbhāvaḥ prajñāyate / yuktyāpi nopapadyate / tathā sati svapnadṛṣṭarūpasya sapratighatvaṃ sanidarśanatvañca bhavet / tena hi hastyādīnāṃ gavākṣādiṣu praveśo nopapadyeta, taddeśasthairapi dṛśyo bhavet / atha sanidarśanaṃ sapratighaṃ ca neṣyate, tadā rūpameva tanna bhavet / nāpyavijñaptiniyamaḥ, tadanabhyupagamāt / yadātmānaṃ bahirgataṃ prekṣate,tadā santānasya dvitvamapi prasajyeta / prāṇyantaradarśane 'pūrvasattvotpattitpattirapi prasajyeta / svapnakṛtābrahmācaryāt pārājikatvamapi prasajyeta / svapnadṛṣṭarūpasya sadbhāvābhyupagame tvevemādayo bahavo doṣā prasajyante // 34 //
body.translated_text: "To refute the opponent, if devoid of reasoning and scripture" and so forth. What is devoid of both reasoning and scripture is an unwholesome position because of its unsoundness. If the <s>Vaibhāṣikas</s> were to adopt it to refute the <s>Yogācāras</s>, [thinking] 'by this they are defeated' — no, because it is unreasonable. Then no one could prevent even the influence of beings of such a kind as maintained by the <s>Yogācāras</s>. For indeed, regarding the beings accepted by you in the dream state, it would have to be said that it is due to their influence that our <s>vijñapti</s>-appearances arise. For that unevenness — being devoid of reasoning and scripture — should be seen thus: from no scripture is the reality of form seen in dreams understood. Nor is it established by reasoning. If it were, then the form seen in dreams would have to be tangible and visible. Then the entry of elephants and the like through windows would be impossible, and it would be visible to those standing in that place. But if it is accepted as neither visible nor tangible, then it would not be form at all. Nor would there be the restriction to non-manifest [form], since that is not accepted. When one perceives oneself as having gone outside, a duality of the [mental] continuum would also follow. In seeing other beings, the arising of unprecedented beings would also follow. From unchaste conduct in dreams, defeat [expulsion from the order] would also follow. If the reality of form seen in dreams is accepted, these and many other faults would follow. || 34 ||

body.text: evaṃ tāvat samānatāṃ prasādhya svapakṣe yuktyāgamarahitatvaṃ parihartumāha -
body.translated_text: Having thus established the similarity, to remove the charge of being devoid of reasoning and scripture in his own position, he says:

body.text: etat keṣāñcinmata eva sarvāṇi tathāvidhāni jñānāni santānāntarāyattāni / viśeṣastu sākṣātparamparayā ca / etat keṣāñcinmata ityādi / etadityāveśenoktam / keṣāzncid yogācārāṇāṃ mata eva jāgradavasthāvat svapne 'pi tathāvidhānī kriyāvāgākārajñānāni parasantānā yattāni bhavanti / viśeṣastu etāvanmātram - jāgradavasthāyāṃ sākṣādāyattāni, svapnāvasthāyāṃ tu prāyeṇa paramparayā // 35 //
body.translated_text: "This is the view of some: all such cognitions depend on other mind-streams. But the distinction is: directly or indirectly." "This is the view of some" and so forth. The word 'this' is said with emphasis. In the view of some <s>Yogācāras</s>, just as in the waking state, so in dreams too, such cognitions having the form of action and speech depend on other mind-streams. But the distinction is only this much: in the waking state they depend directly, while in the dream state they generally depend indirectly. || 35 ||

body.text: svapne 'pi sākṣādvṛtteḥ sambhāvanāṃ pratipādayitumāha -
body.translated_text: To establish the possibility of direct occurrence even in dreams, he says —

body.text:
kadācit svapne 'pi tasya sākṣātsantānāntarāyattatā iṣṭaiva /
kadācit svapne 'pītyādi / sugamametat // 36 //
body.translated_text: Sometimes even in dreams, its direct dependence on another mind-stream is indeed accepted. [The verse says] 'kadācit svapne 'pi' and so forth. This is easy to understand. [Verse 36]

body.text: sākṣādvṛttitvaṃ darśannāha -
body.translated_text: Showing direct occurrence, he says —

body.text: devādyadhiṣṭhānataḥ satyasvapnadarśanāt /
body.translated_text: Because of the empowerment by gods and so forth, there are true dream visions.

body.text: devādyadhiṣṭhānata ityādi / devādyadhiṣṭhānataḥ supriyavaṇijo vijñaptipratibhāsīni jñānāni jāyante ādītyanena yogipiśācādīnāmadhiṣṭhānāni saṃgṛhītāni // 37 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'devādyadhiṣṭhānataḥ' and so forth. Through the empowerment of gods and so forth, cognitions manifesting as <s>vijñapti</s> (representations) arise for the merchant <s>Supriya</s>. By the word 'etc.' (ādi), the empowerments of <s>yogins</s>, <s>piśācas</s> (demons), and others are included. [Verse 37]

body.text: svapakṣamupasaṃharannāha -
body.translated_text: Concluding his own position, he says —

body.text: tasmādasya naitadasadvādasamāśrayaḥ /
body.translated_text: Therefore, for this [<s>Yogācāra</s>], this is neither based on the non-existent nor on the false.

body.text: tasmādasyetyādi / tasmādasyaivaṃvādino yogācārasya nāsadvādasamāśrayaḥ // 38 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'tasmād asya' and so forth. Therefore, for this <s>Yogācāra</s> who holds such a view, the basis is neither on the non-existent nor on the false. [Verse 38]

body.text: punaścāparasmin samānatāṃ sādhayituṃ sautrāntikaṃ pṛcchati -
body.translated_text: And further, in order to establish equality with another [position], he questions the <s>Sautrāntika</s> —

body.text: tāvattayā kriyayāpi taccittaṃ kathaṃ jñāyate?
body.translated_text: Now then, by that action too, how is the other's mind known?

body.text: tāvattayā kriyayetyādi / vijñaptipratibhāsasya gamakatvamityabhimataṃ tāvadavasthāpyam / muhurbhavataiva paryanuyujyate - kasmāt bhavatparikalpitayā tayā kriyayā paracittaṃ jñāyate // 39 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'tāvat tayā kriyayā' and so forth. That <s>vijñapti-pratibhāsa</s> (representation-manifestation) is the indicator — granting this for the time being, you yourself are questioned repeatedly: Why is the other's mind known through the action that you postulate? [Verse 39]

body.text: tathā paryanuyoge sautrāntika āha -
body.translated_text: To this inquiry, the <s>Sautrāntika</s> says —

body.text: cittasya kāryatvāt /
body.translated_text: Because [action] is the effect of mind.

body.text: cittasya kāryatvāditi / yasmāccittasya kāryam, tasmāt sā gamikā // 40 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'cittasya kāryatvāt' — because it is the effect of mind, therefore that [action] is the indicator. [Verse 40]

body.text: siddhāntavādyāha -
body.translated_text: The <s>siddhāntavādin</s> (proponent) says —

body.text: tasya kāryatvaṃ tu cittantare 'pi tulyamiti kathanna jñāyate?
body.translated_text: But that being an effect of mind is equally true of the other [i.e., the cognition] as well — how then is [the other mind] not known [through cognition]?

body.text: tasya kāryatvamityādi kriyā cittasya kāryatvāccittasya gamiketi cet? cittasya tatkāryatvaṃ tu kriyāpratibhāsijñāne 'pi tulyatvāttena kriyāpratibhāsenāpi kasmāt paracittaṃ na jñāyate // 41 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'tasya kāryatvam' and so forth. If action is the indicator of mind because it is the effect of mind — but that being the effect of mind is equally true also in the case of a cognition manifesting action-representations. Therefore, why is the other's mind not known also through that action-representation? [Verse 41]

body.text: siddhāntavādī hetūpasaṃhāravyājena parapratibhāsijñānameva liṅgatvenābhyupagamayitumāha -
body.translated_text: The <s>siddhāntavādin</s>, under the guise of concluding the argument about the reason, says this in order to make [the opponent] accept that cognition manifesting other-representations alone is the inferential sign (<s>liṅga</s>) —

body.text: api ca, yadi tatkriyā svasattāmātreṇa svasantānaṃ pratyāyet, tadānupalabhya mānenāpi syāttathā pratipattiḥ /
body.translated_text: Moreover, if that action, by its mere existence, would indicate its own mind-stream, then even through non-apprehension there would be such an understanding.

body.text: api ca, yadi tatkriyetyādi / kiñceyaṃ kriyā sattāmātrāt paracittamavabodhayed ohosvit jñānāt? yadi tāvad sattāmātrāditi, tadā kriyāmanupalabhyamānenāpi prāṇinā paracitta pratipadyeta // 42 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'api ca, yadi tatkriyā' and so forth. Furthermore, does this action make known the other's mind from its mere existence, or from cognition? If from mere existence, then even a being who does not apprehend the action would understand the other's mind. [Verse 42]

body.text: paramatamāśaṅkyāha -
body.translated_text: Anticipating the opponent's view, he says —

body.text: na; jñānāpekṣatvālliṅgasyeti cet /
body.translated_text: Objection: No, because the inferential sign (<s>liṅga</s>) is dependent on cognition.

body.text: na; jñānāpekṣatvādityādi / na hi liṅgaṃ sattāmātrāt gamakaṃ bhavati / kiṃ tarhi? jñānāt / tasmānnāyaṃ doṣaḥ // 43 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'na; jñānāpekṣatvāt' and so forth. For the inferential sign is not an indicator from mere existence. From what then? From cognition. Therefore this is not a fault. [Verse 43]

body.text: siddhāntavādyāha -
body.translated_text: The <s>siddhāntavādin</s> says —

body.text: tadā tatra kimanayā paramparayā - paracittāt kriyā, kriyātaḥ jñānam, jñānāttasya pratipattiriti /
body.translated_text: Then what is the use of this chain: from the other's mind arises action, from action arises cognition, from cognition arises the understanding of that [other mind]?

body.text: tadā tatretyādi syānmatam - liṅga jñānamapekṣya gamakamiti / hanta, tarhi na kiñcit prayojanamanayā paramparayā / tāṃ paramparāṃ darśayannāha - paracittāt kriyetyādi / paramparā tu paracittāt kriyā utpadyate, kriyātaḥ jñānam, jñānāttasya pratipattiriti // 44 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'tadā tatra' and so forth. It might be thought that the inferential sign is an indicator dependent on cognition. Well then, there is no purpose served by this chain. Showing the chain, he says 'paracittāt kriyā' and so forth: the chain is — from the other's mind, action arises; from action, cognition; from cognition, the understanding of that [other mind]. [Verse 44]

body.text: kaśya punarnyāya iti cedāha -
body.translated_text: If one asks what the rationale is, he says —

body.text: paracittaprabhavadharmi kriyāpratibhāsijñānamevāsya gamakaṃ bhavati /
body.translated_text: The cognition manifesting action-representations, which has the property of originating from the other's mind, alone is the indicator of this.

body.text: paracittaprabhavadharmītyādi / paracittaprabhavadharmi kriyāpratibhāsijñānameva gamakamiti manvīta / paracittaprabhavadharmo 'syāstīti vigrahaḥ // 45 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'paracittaprabhavadharmi' and so forth. One might hold that the cognition manifesting action-representations, which has the property of originating from the other's mind, alone is the indicator. The compound analysis: that which has the property of originating from the other's mind — this is the analysis. [Verse 45]

body.text: kriyetyapi yujyeta, kriyāpratibhāsijñānamityapi yujyeta / kaścātra viśeṣaḥ? tasmād āha -
body.translated_text: It could be [argued that] 'action' is suitable, or 'cognition manifesting action-representations' is suitable. What is the difference here? Therefore he says —

body.text: tasyādhigatistvantaśastadāśritatvāt /
body.translated_text: But the understanding of that [other mind] is ultimately dependent on that [cognition], because it rests upon it.

body.text: tasyādhigatistvantaśa ityādi / yato hyabhyupagatāyāmapi kriyāyāṃ paracittasyādhigatistu kriyāpratibhāsijñānādhīnaiva / tasmāttadevāstu / kimanayā parikalpitayā kriyayā // 46 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'tasyādhigatiḥ tu antaśaḥ' and so forth. Since, even when action is accepted, the understanding of the other's mind is ultimately dependent on the cognition manifesting action-representations alone. Therefore, let that alone [be the indicator]. What use is this postulated action? [Verse 46]

body.text: evaṃ paraṃ nigṛhya svamatamākhyātumāha -
body.translated_text: Having thus refuted the opponent, to declare his own position, he says —

body.text: spandanamātrasāmānyāṃ kriyābhilāpajñānasāmānyasya kāraṇatvāt kāryeṇa lāraṇasya gatiḥ / spandanamātrasāmānyaṃ kriyābhilāpajñānasāmānyasyetyādi / kriyābhilāpajñānasya sāmānyaṃ kriyābhilāpajñānasāmānyam / tasya kāraṇaṃ tvaviśeṣeṇa spandanamātramiṣṭam / tathā sati kriyāpratibhāsijñānasāmānyaṃ spandanamātrasāmānyasya gamakamiṣyate / ata eva uktam - kāryeṇa karaṇasya gati iti / jñānasāmānyetyatra sāmānyeti śabdena vicchinnāvicchinnapratibhāsakṛtaviśeṣaḥ nirākṛtaḥ / spandanamātretyatra mātreti śabdena rāgādikṛtaviśiṣṭaspandanaṃ nirākriyate // 47 //
body.translated_text: The general characteristic of mere impulse is the cause of the general characteristic of action-and-speech cognition; and the cause is known through the effect. [The verse says] 'spandanamātrasāmānyaṃ kriyābhilāpajñānasāmānyasya' and so forth. The general characteristic of action-and-speech cognition — the general characteristic of that is 'action-and-speech cognition general characteristic.' Its cause is accepted to be mere impulse without distinction. This being so, the general characteristic of cognition manifesting action-representations is accepted as the indicator of the general characteristic of mere impulse. Hence it is said: the cause is known through the effect. In the expression 'general characteristic of cognition,' the word 'general characteristic' removes the distinction created by discontinuous and continuous manifestation. In 'mere impulse,' the word 'mere' removes impulse qualified by attachment and so forth. [Verse 47]

body.text: evaṃ sāmānyena kāryakāraṇabhāvaṃ nirdiśya kāryasya bhedamupadarśayitumāha -
body.translated_text: Having thus indicated the causal relation in general, in order to show the differentiation of the effect, he says —

body.text: tatra ātmaspandananimittakasyāntarmukhavṛttiḥ, anyasyānyathā / prāyeṇādhikṛtya asau bhedaḥ /
body.translated_text: Therein, [the cognition] caused by one's own impulse has an inward-directed functioning, while that of another functions otherwise. Generally, this distinction is based on [the subject matter] under discussion.

body.text: tatra ātmaspandananimittakasyetyādi / ātmaspandanātsamutthitaṃ yajjñānaṃ tasyāntarmukhapratibhāsatayā vṛttiḥ, paraspandanātsamutthitasya tu bahirmukhapratibhāsatayā / mukheti śabdo 'trālambane vartate / prāyeṇādhikṛtyetyanena śaraprakṣepaṇādīnāaṃ parakṛtacālanādīnāṃ ca pradarśanam / 48 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'tatra ātmaspandananimittakasya' and so forth. The cognition that arises from one's own impulse has its functioning through inward-facing manifestation; while that which arises from another's impulse has outward-facing manifestation. The word 'mukha' (face/direction) here refers to the object (<s>ālambana</s>). By 'generally, based on [the subject matter] under discussion,' he indicates examples such as the hurling of arrows, movements caused by others, and so forth. [Verse 48]

body.text: tatra syānmatam - bhavatu jāgradavasthāyāṃ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ, svapnāvasthāyāṃ tu tatkathamiti cet?
body.translated_text: At this point one might think: granted, the causal relation holds in the waking state, but how does it apply in the dream state? To this —

body.text: āha -
body.translated_text: He says —

body.text: etayoḥ saḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ svāpādyavasthāyāmitarasyāmapi ca samānaḥ / etayoḥ saḥ kāryakāraṇabhāva ityādi / yaścānantaroktaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ, saḥ svāpajāgradavasthayośca samānaḥ / ādītyanena kāmaśokādibhirupahatāvasthānāṃ parigrahaḥ // 49 //
body.translated_text: The causal relation between these two is the same in the sleeping and other states as well. [The verse says] 'etayoḥ saḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ' and so forth. The causal relation just stated above is the same in both the sleeping and waking states. By the word 'etc.' (ādi), states affected by desire, grief, and so forth are included. [Verse 49]

body.text: nanu svapne samutthāpakaspandanameva nāsti / tatkathaṃ kāryakāraṇabhāvasya samānateti / tasmādāha -
body.translated_text: Objection: In dreams, there is no originating impulse at all. How then can the causal relation be the same? Therefore he says —

body.text: bhrāntyavasthāyāṃ yathāsvaṃ pratyayaviśeṣopāśrayāt paraspandanādinimittodbhūtavijñānavāsanaiva kadācitparābhogādeḥ vyavahitādapi vṛttiṃ labhate, na tu atyantāsadābhogāt /
body.translated_text: In the state of delusion, depending on its own respective special condition, the latent impression (<s>vāsanā</s>) of the cognition that originally arose from the impulse of another and so forth sometimes obtains functioning even from a remote engagement with the other, but not from an engagement with what is utterly non-existent.

body.text: bhrāntyavasthāyāmityādi / bhrāntyavasthāyāmiti middhenopahatādyavasthāyām / yathāsvamityanena svapnasya middhaviśeṣaḥ, narakādeḥ karmavipākāvasthā ca parogṛhyate / pratyayaviśeṣo middhādiḥ / upāśrayaṇam upāśrayaḥ / pratyayaviśeṣasya upāśrayaḥ pratyayaviśeṣopāśrayaḥ / pratyayaviśeṣamupāśrayata iti yāvat / paracittena saṃprayuktaṃ spandanaṃ paraspandanam / ādītyanena mukhakāntiraktimādīnāṃ janakacittasya paroigrahaḥ paraspandanādi ca nimittaṃ ceti samāsaḥ / nimittatvamatrādhipatipratyayatvamiti draṣṭavyam / yasya kriyādipratibhāsivijñānasya tadanyasmāt spandanādinimittādudbhavituṃ śīlamasti tat paraspandādinimittodbhūtavijñānam / tasya vāsanā śaktiḥ / parābhogaḥ paramanaskāraḥ ādītyanena tatkālabhāvināṃ tadanyapratyayānāṃ parigrahaḥ / vyavahitaḥ kālaviprakṛṣṭaḥ / apīti śabdo 'vyavahite devādyadhiṣṭhānāt svapnadarśane 'pi / tasyāḥ vṛttilābhaḥ kriyāpratibhāsivijñānajananayogyātmatayā samavadhānam / evamuktaṃ bhavati - bhrāntyavasthāyāṃ pratyayaviśeṣasya upāśrayāt paraspandanādinimittadudbhūtavijñānavāsanā kadācit vyavahitād parābhogādapi vṛttiṃ labhate / yasyāstu parābhogo 'tyantāsanna tasmād vṛttiṃ labhate // 50 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'bhrāntyavasthāyām' and so forth. 'In the state of delusion' means in a state affected by torpor (<s>middha</s>) and so forth. By 'its own respective,' <s>svapna</s> (dream) is taken as a variety of torpor, and the state of karmic ripening for hell-beings and others is also included. 'Special condition' means torpor and so forth. 'Dependence' means reliance. 'Dependence on the special condition' means relying on the special condition — that is, relying on the special condition [as the supporting cause]. 'Impulse connected with another mind' is 'other-impulse' (<s>paraspandana</s>). By the word 'etc.' (ādi), cognitions generating facial glow, reddening, and so forth are included. 'Other-impulse etc.' and 'cause' form a compound. Causality here should be understood as <s>adhipatipratyayatva</s> (dominant conditioning). The cognition that has the disposition to arise from impulse and other causes, whose manifestation is of actions and such — that is 'cognition arisen from other-impulse etc.' Its <s>vāsanā</s> (latent impression) is its capacity. 'Other's engagement' means another's mental attending (<s>manaskāra</s>). By the word 'etc.' (ādi), other conditions existing at that time are included. 'Remote' means distant in time. The word 'also' (api) [indicates] even in the case of non-remote [engagement], as in dream visions through the empowerment of gods and so forth. The obtaining of functioning by that [<s>vāsanā</s>] is the readiness for generating cognition manifesting action-representations. Thus it has been said: in the state of delusion, due to dependence on the special condition, the latent impression of the cognition arisen from other-impulse etc. sometimes obtains functioning even from a remote engagement of the other. But from an engagement that is utterly non-existent, it does not obtain functioning. [Verse 50]

body.text: evaṃ svapnāvasthāyāmapi kriyāpratibhāsijñānānāṃ spandananimittakatvaṃ sādhayitvā upasaṃhartum āha -
body.translated_text: Having thus established that even in the dream state, cognitions manifesting action-representations are caused by impulse, in order to conclude, he says —

body.text: tasmāt sarvāvasthāsu kriyādivijñapteḥ cittaspandanamanumīyata eva /
body.translated_text: Therefore, in all states, from the representation (<s>vijñapti</s>) of actions and so forth, mental impulse (<s>cittaspandana</s>) is indeed inferred.

body.text: tasmāt sarvāvasthāsvityādi yasmādevamavyabhicāritvaṃ sādhitam, tasmāt svāpajāgradubhayorapyavasthayoḥ kriyāpratibhāsāt cittaspandanamanumīyata eveti sthitam / ādi ityanena abhilāparaktimādivijñaptīnāṃ parigrahaḥ // 51 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'tasmāt sarvāvasthāsu' and so forth. Since non-deviation has thus been established, therefore in both the sleeping and waking states, from the manifestation of action-representations, mental impulse is indeed inferred — this is established. By the word 'etc.' (ādi), representations of speech, facial glow, and so forth are included. [Verse 51]

body.text: evaṃ svamataṃ nirdoṣīkṛtya paramate doṣamudbhāvayitumāha -
body.translated_text: Having thus made his own position free from fault, in order to raise a fault against the opponent's position, he says —

body.text: kriyātaḥ spandanapratipattau svāpa itarasmiñca syāt pratipattiratha vā naiva kadācana /
body.translated_text: If impulse is inferred from action, then the inference should hold also in sleep and in the other [waking] state — or else never at all.

body.text: kriyātaḥ spandanapratipattāvityādi / yamnate kriyātaḥ spandanasya pratipattiḥ, tanmate svpnādāvapi kriyātaḥ spandanasya pratipattirbhavet / atha svapne kriyātaḥ spandanasya pratipattirneṣyeta, tadā tat jāgradavasthāyāmapi yujyeta na kadāciyt kriyātaḥ spandanasya pratipattirbhavediti vākyaśeṣaḥ // 52 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'kriyātaḥ spandanapratipattau' and so forth. In that view where impulse is inferred from action, in that view the inference of impulse from action should hold even in dreams and such states. If the inference of impulse from action is not accepted in dreams, then it would also follow that in the waking state too — the implied completion is: the inference of impulse from action would never hold. [Verse 52]

body.text: kathamiti cet? tasmādāha -
body.translated_text: How so? Therefore he says —

body.text: paraspandanābhāve 'pi kriyālambanodayāt /
body.translated_text: Because cognitions with action as their object arise even in the absence of another's impulse.

body.text: paraspandanābhāve 'pītyādi / tathāhi, svapne paracittaspandanābhāve 'pi kriyālambanam udeti / yasyābhāve 'pi yadutpadyate, na tattasya gamakaṃ yuktaṃ // 53 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'paraspandanābhāve 'pi' and so forth. Indeed, in dreams, even in the absence of another mind's impulse, cognitions with action as their object arise. That which arises even in the absence of something is not reasonably an indicator of that thing. [Verse 53]

body.text: pratividhātukāmo bāhyārthavādyāha -
body.translated_text: The <s>bāhyārthavādin</s> (external realist), wishing to counter, says —

body.text: bhavatvālambanodayaḥ, na tu kriyā / kriyayā spandanaṃ gamyete / bhrāntyavasthāyāṃ kriyaiva na bhavati / arthaśūnyajñānodayānna doṣaḥ /
body.translated_text: Granted, there is the arising of objects of cognition, but not of real action. Impulse is indicated by action. In the state of delusion, action itself does not exist. There is no fault, since cognitions empty of real objects arise.

body.text: bhavatvālambanodayarityādi / ālambanaṃ tu spandanābhāve 'pyutpadyate, na tu kriyā / asmākaṃ mate kriyā spandanasya gamakam / sā ca bhrāntyavasthāyāṃ na bhavati / kathaṃ na bhavati? āha - arthaśūnyajñānodayāditi / yasmāt bhrāntyavasthāyāmarthaśūnyāni jñānāni utpadhyante, tasmānnaiṣa doṣa iti pūrvapakṣāśaṅkā // 54 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'bhavatvālambanodayaḥ' and so forth. Objects of cognition do arise even in the absence of impulse, but not real action. In our view, action is the indicator of impulse. And that [action] does not exist in the state of delusion. How does it not exist? He says: 'because cognitions empty of real objects arise.' Since in the state of delusion cognitions empty of real objects arise, therefore this is not a fault — this is the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (opponent's objection). [Verse 54]

body.text: siddhantavādyāha -
body.translated_text: The <s>siddhāntavādin</s> (proponent) says —

body.text: sarvaprakāravyapadeśasāmyāt kadācijjñānamarthaśūnyam, anyadānyathetyeṣo 'dhikāraḥ kuto labdhaḥ? sarvaprakāravyapadeśasāmyādityādi / yasya vyapadeśasya santi sarve prakārāḥ sa sarvaprakāravyapadeśaḥ / sarvaprakāravyapadeśasāmye svapnāvasthāyāṃ jñānamarthaśūnyamutpadyate, jāgradavasthāyāṃ tu sārthamityetat jñānam, adhikāro vā bhavatā kuto labdhaḥ? evamuktaṃ bhavati - jāgradavasthāvat svapnāvasthāyāmapi dṛśyākārādayaḥ sarve santi / tatkathaṃ tatra jñānamarthaśūnyamiti // 55 //
body.translated_text: Since in all respects the designation is the same, by what authority is it obtained that some cognitions are empty of objects while others are otherwise? [The verse says] 'sarvaprakāravyapadeśasāmyāt' and so forth. A designation that has all characteristics is a designation of all kinds. When the designation is the same in all respects, in the dream state cognition arises empty of objects, while in the waking state it has real objects — by what authority, or how, is this knowledge obtained by you? This is what is said: just as in the waking state, in the dream state also all features such as the appearance of visible forms are present. Then how can it be that cognition there is empty of real objects? [Verse 55]

body.text: paramatamāśaṅkitumāha -
body.translated_text: Raising the opponent's view, he says —

body.text: atha middhādināvasthānyathābhāvaścet /
body.translated_text: Objection: Because of the condition of sleep and such, there is an alteration of state.

body.text: atha middhādinetyādi / yathāsyāmavasthāyāṃ middhadinārthaśūnyajñānānāmutpattirbhavati, tathā anyathābhāva it pūrvapakṣāśaṅkā // 56 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'atha middhādina' and so forth. Just as in this state, due to sleep and such, cognitions empty of real objects arise, so there is an alteration of state — this is the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (opponent's objection). [Verse 56]

body.text: siddhāntavādyāha -
body.translated_text: The <s>siddhāntavādin</s> (proponent) says —

body.text: yadyevaṃ sambhavet, bhavatu avidyoipaplutatvāttathodayaḥ /
body.translated_text: If that were so, let it be that due to being overwhelmed by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), cognitions arise in that manner.

body.text: yadyevaṃ sambhavedityādi / yadi bhrāntivaśādavasthānyathābhāvādarthaśūnyaṃ jñānaṃ jāyata iti abhyupāgamyeta, tadā mahābhramarājñyā avidyāyāḥ sadbhāvāt tadvaśācca sarvāṇi jñānānyarthaśūnyāni jāyanta iti manyeran // 57 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'yadyevaṃ sambhavet' and so forth. If it were accepted that due to the power of delusion and the alteration of state, cognition arises empty of real objects, then due to the existence of <s>avidyā</s>, the great queen of delusions, and due to its power, one would have to accept that all cognitions arise empty of real objects. [Verse 57]

body.text: tathā sati ko guṇaḥ? āha -
body.translated_text: If that were so, what advantage would there be? He says —

body.text: tathā satyarthāntaravādahānyā ete 'nekāśakyanigūhanāvatārāḥ mahākṛcchrā uttareṇaikena nihatā bhavanti / tathā satyarthāntaravādetyādi / arthāntaraṃ vadatīti arthāntaravādaḥ / arthāntaravādasyaiva hānyā arthāntaravādahānyā / asya kṣemadharmebhyaścyutatvādayukto bhavati / yasmārthāntaravādasya aneke avatārāḥ doṣāḥ parihāralakṣaṇenāśakyanigūhanāḥ santyamī anekāśakyanigūhanāvatārāḥ / mahāntaḥ kṛcchrāḥ santyasyeti mahākṛcchrāḥ / uttereṇaikeneti ekasmāduttarāt / nihatāḥ nirākṛtāḥ / aśakyanigūhanāvatāratvaṃ tu kṛte ekasya parihāre 'nyānyadoṣodbhavāt / evamuktaṃ bhavati - yadāvidyopaplutatvāt sarveṣāṃ jñānānāmarthaśūnyatvamabhyupagamyate, tadārthāntaravādasya ye 'nekāśakyanigūhanāvatārāsta uttareṇaikena nirākṛtā bhavanti // 58 //
body.translated_text: That being so, through the destruction of the 'changing the subject' fallacy, these numerous objections that cannot be hidden by any means, which are great difficulties, are all destroyed by this single response. [The verse says] 'tathā satyarthāntaravāda' and so forth. One who speaks of another matter is an <s>arthāntaravādin</s> (one guilty of the 'changing the subject' fallacy). The destruction of the changing-the-subject argument itself is the 'destruction of the changing-the-subject argument.' His being fallen from wholesome dharmas makes it untenable. Since the changing-the-subject argument has numerous entry points of faults that cannot be hidden through any means of refutation — these are the 'numerous unhideable entry points.' Those that have great difficulties — those are 'of great difficulty.' 'By a single response' means by one response. 'Destroyed' means refuted. The nature of having unhideable entry points is due to the arising of fresh faults each time one fault is refuted. This is what is said: when it is accepted that due to being overwhelmed by <s>avidyā</s>, all cognitions are empty of real objects, then the numerous unhideable entry points of the changing-the-subject argument are all refuted by this single response. [Verse 58]

body.text: evaṃ santānāntarasiddhiṃ parisamāpyāvaśiṣṭān durupālambhān parihartukāmaḥ paramatamāśaṅkitum āha -
body.translated_text: Having thus completed the proof of other mind-streams, wishing to address remaining difficult objections, he raises the opponent's view —

body.text: nanu tayoḥ darśanāt kāyavāgvijñaptibhyāṃ svamutthāpakacittasyānumānamiti nyāyyam / na tu santānāntarasambaddhavijñāptipratibhāsijñāne paravijñaptī bhavitumarhataḥ, tayoranupādānopādeyatvāditi cet /
body.translated_text: Objection: Is it not reasonable that from seeing those two [actions and speech], through bodily and verbal <s>vijñapti</s> (representations), the mind that produced them is inferred? But in a cognition in another mind-stream that manifests as the representation of another, the two <s>vijñaptis</s> cannot exist, because there is no relationship of material cause and effect between them.

body.text: nanu tayoḥ darśanātkāyavāgvijñaptibhyāmityādi / nanvityanenākṣamyatāṃ darśayati / nanu kāyavāgvijñaptipratibhāsābhyāṃ tayoḥ samutthāpakacittasyānumānamiti nyāyyam / tatra syānmatam - etadapi samānamiti / ata āha - santānāntarasambaddhetyādi / ye ca śrotṛsantānasambaddhavijñaptipratibhāsijñāne spandanasya gamake iti bhavadbhiriṣṭe, kathaṃ te vaktuḥ vijñaptī syātām? atra santāneti śrotuḥ santānaḥ / tamapekṣya antareti śabdena vaktuḥ parigrahaḥ / kasmānnārhataḥ? ityāha - tayoḥ anupādānopādeyatvāditi / ayamabhiprāyaḥ - śrotṛsantānapratibaddhavijñaptipratibhāsasya na vaktuḥ vivakṣayā sahopādānopādeyabhāvaḥ, bhinnasantānaparyāppannatvāditi pūrvapakṣaḥ // 59 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'nanu tayoḥ darśanāt kāyavāgvijñaptibhyām' and so forth. By 'nanu' he shows disapproval. Is it not reasonable that from the two — the manifestation of bodily and verbal representations — the mind that produced them is inferred? One might think: this too is the same [as our position]. Therefore he says 'santānāntarasambaddha' and so forth. If in your view, in cognitions in the listener's mind-stream that manifest representations, these serve as indicators of impulse, how could they be the speaker's <s>vijñaptis</s>? Here 'mind-stream' refers to the listener's mind-stream. In relation to that, by the word 'other,' the speaker is included. Why can they not be? He says: because there is no relationship of material cause and effect between them. The intent is: the manifestation of representations connected with the listener's mind-stream does not have a material cause-effect relationship with the speaker's intention, because they belong to different mind-streams — this is the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (opponent's position). [Verse 59]

body.text: tatra siddhāntavādyāha -
body.translated_text: To this, the <s>siddhāntavādin</s> (proponent) says —

body.text: nocyate paracittasamitthitavijñaptirūpatvāt tatra pratibhāsijñānena samutthāpakacittaṃ gamyata iti / kiṃ tarhi? tasya kāryatvāt /
body.translated_text: We do not say that through cognition manifesting there the nature of representation produced by another mind, the producing mind is inferred. Rather, [it is inferred] because it is an effect of that [other mind].

body.text: nocyata ityādi / paracittena samutthitā paracittasamitthitā / paracittasamitthitā ca vijñaptiśceti paracittasamutthitavijñaptiḥ / sā yasya pratibhāsino jñānasya rūpaṃ svabhāvo 'sti tattathā / tasya bhāvaḥ tattvam / tasmāt paracittasamutthitavijñaptirūpatvāt / tatra vijñapteḥ pratibhāso 'syāstīti pratibhāsi / evamuktaṃ bhavati - yasmāt tatra pratibhāsi jñānaṃ paracittasamutthitavijñaptirūpam, tasmāt samutthāpakacittaṃ gamyata iti vayamapi nābhyupagacchāmaḥ / yadi nābhyupagamyate, kiṃ tarhi abhyupagamyata iti cet? āha - kiṃ tarhi? tasya kāryatvād iti / yasmād vijñaptipratibhāsijñānaṃ paracittasya kāryam, tasmāt paracittaṃ gamyate / atra paracittaṃ vaktuścittamabhipretam // 60 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'nocyate' and so forth. Produced by another mind — that is 'other-mind-produced.' That which is other-mind-produced and is a representation — that is 'other-mind-produced representation.' That which is the nature or essential character of a cognition that manifests it — that is so. The state of being that is its nature. Therefore, because of having the nature of representation produced by another mind. There, that which has manifestation of representation — that is 'manifesting.' This is what is said: since the manifesting cognition there has the nature of representation produced by another mind, we too do not accept that the producing mind is thereby inferred. If it is not accepted, then what is accepted? He says: 'Rather, because it is an effect of that [other mind].' Since the cognition manifesting representation is an effect of the other mind, therefore the other mind is inferred. Here 'other mind' refers to the speaker's mind. [Verse 60]

body.text: yadi śrotṛsantānājjāte kriyāvāgākārake jñāne vijñaptitvena neṣyete, kā punaranyā vijñaptiścet / tasmādāha -
