body.translated_text: If it is not accepted that cognitions with the form of actions and speech arising in the listener's mind-stream are <s>vijñaptis</s> (representations), then what else is <s>vijñapti</s>? Therefore he says —

body.text: vijñaptiriti samutthāpakacittasantānājjāte kriyāvāgākārake jñāne eva / vijñaptirityādi / samutthāpakacittasantānājjāte ye kriyāvāgākārake jñāne te vijñaptitvena vyapadiśyete / evamuktaṃ bhavati - vaktureva ye gamanābhilāpane kriyāvāgākārake jñāne te vijñaptīti ucyete // 61 //
body.translated_text: <s>Vijñapti</s> (representation) refers precisely to cognitions with the form of actions and speech that arise from the mind-stream of the producing mind. [The verse says] 'vijñaptir' and so forth. Those cognitions with the form of actions and speech that arise from the mind-stream of the producing mind — those are designated as <s>vijñaptis</s>. This is what is said: only those cognitions with the form of movement and speech belonging to the speaker himself are called <s>vijñaptis</s>. [Verse 61]

body.text: samutthāpakacittaṃ svaparasantānagatayoḥ kriyāvāgākārakajñāneyoryathā kāraṇabhāvo bhavati taddarśayitumāha -
body.translated_text: To show how the producing mind serves as a cause for cognitions with the form of actions and speech in both one's own and another's mind-stream, he says —

body.text: samutthāpakacittaṃ ca tayorevopādānakāraṇam, santānāntarajñānayostu adhipatipratyayaḥ / samutthāpakacittam ca tayorityādi / upādānākāraṇamasādhāraṇakāraṇe vartate / samutthāpakacittaṃ svasantānagatayoḥ kriyāvāgākārakayorevopādānakāraṇam, parasantānasambaddhayostvadhipatipratyayaḥ / taccopādānakāraṇaṃ paratamapekṣya upanyastam / svamate tu upādānakāraṇamālayavijñānamiṣyate, na tu vivakṣācittam // 62 //
body.translated_text: The producing mind is the <s>upādānakāraṇa</s> (material cause) of those very [cognitions in its own stream], while for cognitions in another mind-stream it is the <s>adhipatipratyaya</s> (dominant condition). [The verse says] 'samutthāpakacittaṃ ca tayoḥ' and so forth. <s>Upādānakāraṇa</s> applies in the sense of the uncommon cause. The producing mind is the material cause only of cognitions with the form of actions and speech in its own mind-stream, while for those connected with another mind-stream it is the dominant condition. And this material cause is stated in relation to the other [system]. In our own view, the <s>ālayavijñāna</s> (storehouse consciousness) is accepted as the material cause, not the intentional mind. [Verse 62]

body.text: evaṃ tāvat svasantānāgatayoḥ kriyāvāgākārakayorvijñaptivaṃ pratipāditam / santānāntarasaṃbaddhayośca sādhayitumāha -
body.translated_text: Having thus established the status of <s>vijñapti</s> for cognitions with the form of actions and speech in one's own mind-stream, in order to establish it for those connected with another mind-stream, he says —

body.text: vijñapterūpādānātte janite / tatsambandhenopacārād vijñaptī bhavataḥ / vijñapterūpādānātte janite ityādi / vijñapteryadupādānakāraṇaṃ tena te santānāntarasambaddhakriyāvāgākārake jñāne janite / tajjanisambandhena tena hetunā upacārād vijñaptīti vyapadiśyete // 63 //
body.translated_text: They are produced from the material cause of <s>vijñapti</s>. Through the connection with that, by figurative designation they are <s>vijñaptis</s>. [The verse says] 'vijñapterupādānāt te janite' and so forth. Those cognitions with the form of actions and speech connected with another mind-stream are produced by that which is the material cause of <s>vijñapti</s>. Through the connection of being produced by that cause, by figurative designation they are designated as <s>vijñaptis</s>. [Verse 63]

body.text: syānmatam - svasamutthāpakacittasya vijñāpanād vijñaptiḥ / na hi śrotā vaktṛsantānājjāte kriyāvākpratibhāsijñāne upalabhate / tathā hi, vaktā śrotā cobhāvapi svasvapratibhāsamanu bhavataḥ / tatkathaṃ te 'nālambane vijñaptitvena svasamutthāpakasya gamake iti / tasmādāha -
body.translated_text: Perhaps [the objection is]: <s>vijñapti</s> (expression) is the making-known (<s>vijñāpana</s>) of the mind that originates it in one's own [continuum]. For the hearer does not apprehend in the cognition arising from the speaker's continuum in which actions and speech appear. For indeed, both the speaker and the hearer experience only their own respective appearances. Then how are those [cognitions], as expressions, indicators of the mind that originates them, when they do not have [the other's mind] as their object? Therefore he says—

body.text: bhavatu svaparayoḥ svasvapratibhāsasyānubhavaḥ, taimirikadvayadṛṣṭadvicandravat / tathāvidhavijñānasya hetuḥ vāsanotpādasvabhāvaviśeṣo 'nādikālikaikārthagrāhādhyavasāyitvāt, ekahetusambhūtayoḥ svaparavijñaptijñānayoḥ vijñaptitvena upacāraḥ /
body.translated_text: Let there be the experience of one's own respective appearances for both self and other, like two moons seen by two persons with eye-disease (<s>taimirika</s>). The cause of such cognition is a particular kind of latent impression (<s>vāsanā</s>) arising, which from beginningless time apprehends and determines a single object; between the cognitions of self-expression and other-expression that arise from a single cause, the designation as 'expression' (<s>vijñapti</s>) is figurative.

body.text: bhavatu svaparayorityādi / svapareti vaktā śrotā ca / svasya svasya pratibhāsasya anubhavaḥ svasvapratibhāsasyānubhavaḥ / taimirikadvayena pratibhāsasyānubhavaḥ taimirikadvayadṛṣṭadvicandram / tena tulyatvāt tadvat / tathāvidhavijñānamiti ekārthagrāhādhyavasāyi vijñānaṃ matam / tasya hetuḥ ekārthagrāhādhyavasāyasyānubhavitṛ pūrvavijñānam / tajjanitā vāsanā śaktirūpā / tasyā utpāda utpādavyayalakṣaṇaparamparāyā udayaḥ / svarūpa utpādasvabhāvaḥ / tasya viśeṣa ekārthagrāhādhyavasāyivijñānopajanane samarthātmani sthitiḥ /
body.translated_text: 'Let there be for self and other' and so forth. 'Self and other' means the speaker and the hearer. The experience of one's own respective appearances is 'the experience of one's own appearances.' The experience of appearances by two persons with eye-disease is 'the two moons seen by two persons with eye-disease.' Due to similarity with that, 'like that.' 'Such cognition' means the cognition that apprehends and determines a single object. Its cause is the prior cognition that experiences the apprehension and determination of a single object. The <s>vāsanā</s> (latent impression) born from that has the form of a capacity (<s>śakti</s>). Its 'arising' is the emergence of the series characterized by origination and cessation. Its inherent nature is the 'arising-nature.' Its 'particular' is its stability in the capacity to generate the cognition that apprehends and determines a single object.

body.text: anādiścāsau kālaśceti anādikālaḥ / tasmādāgato 'nādikālikaḥ / atha vānādikāle bhavo 'nādikālikaḥ / na ādikālikaḥ anādikālikaḥ / ekaścāsau arthaśceti ekārthaḥ / gamanavāgādisvaparavijñaptyoḥ buddhyā ekīkaraṇam / ekārthagrāheti ekārthagrāhijñānam / ekārthagrāhādhyavasāyi iti adhyavasāyijñānam / tathā hi, vaktā caivaṃ cintayati - yanmayā kathitaṃ tat śrotrā jñātam / śrotāpyevaṃ cintayati - yadanena kathitaṃ tanmayā pratītam / ityevaṃ ekārthagrāhādhyavasāyaḥ /
body.translated_text: 'Beginningless' (<s>anādi</s>) and 'time' (<s>kāla</s>) [combine as] 'beginningless time.' Coming from that is 'from beginningless time.' Or alternatively, existing in beginningless time is 'beginningless-in-time.' Not having a beginning in time is 'beginningless-in-time.' 'Single' and 'object' [combine as] 'single object'—the mental unification by the intellect of the self- and other-expressions of movement, speech, and so forth. 'Apprehending a single object' means the cognition that apprehends a single object. 'Apprehending and determining a single object' means the cognition that determines. For indeed, the speaker thinks thus: 'What I have said, the hearer has understood.' The hearer too thinks thus: 'What he has said, I have understood.' This is the apprehension and determination of a single object.

body.text: ekahetunā samutthāpakena ye sambhūte te ekahetusambhūte / svaparavijñaptijñānayoḥ vaktṛśrotṛkriyāvāgākārakajñānayoḥ vijñaptitvenopacāraḥ vijñaptitvena vyapadeśaḥ / evaṃ vaktā śrotā ca svasvapratibhāsamanubhavataḥ / tathāpi tayoḥ ya ekahetusambhūte kriyāvāgākārakajñāne ta ekārthapratītiniyamād vijñaptitvena vyapadiśyete /
body.translated_text: 'Arisen from a single cause' (<s>ekahetusambhūta</s>)—those that are produced by a single originating cause are arisen from a single cause. Of the cognitions of self-expression and other-expression—that is, the cognitions of the speaker and hearer having the form of action and speech—the designation as expression is figurative, meaning the verbal designation as expression. Thus the speaker and hearer experience their own respective appearances. Nevertheless, because those two cognitions of the form of action and speech arise from a single cause, they are designated as expressions due to the invariable determination of a single object.

body.text: ekārthagrāhādhyavasāyastu tathāvidhavijñānasya heturvāsanotpādasvabhāvaviśeṣo 'nādikālikatvād / taimirikadvayadṛṣṭadvicandravaditi dṛṣṭāntaḥ / ekaḥ taimirikaḥ dvitīyaṃ taimirikaṃ 'paśya' iti "aparaṃ candraṃ' darśayati / tena ca 'dṛśyate" ityucyate / tatra 'mayā asmaidarśitaḥ' ityevaṃ darśakasyābhimāno bhavati / śrotāpi 'anena mahyaṃ darśitaḥ iti cintayati / tathāpi tau svasvapratibhāsaṃ prativittaḥ / tadvadatrāpi ekārthapratītiniyamāt svaparavijñaptijñānayorvijñaptitvenopacāro bhavati // 64 //
body.translated_text: The apprehension and determination of a single object is indeed the cause of such cognition—a particular arising of a latent impression—because it is from beginningless time. 'Like two moons seen by two persons with eye-disease' is the example. One person with eye-disease shows a second person with eye-disease [saying] 'look'—'another moon.' And the other 'sees' it, as is said. Therein the shower has the conceit: 'I showed this to him.' The hearer also thinks: 'He showed it to me.' Nevertheless, the two experienced only their own respective appearances. Likewise here too, due to the invariable determination of a single object, the designation of the cognitions of self- and other-expression as expression is figurative. [Verse 64]

body.text: tṛṇāvalambina iva bāhyārthabādinaḥ prāhuḥ -
body.translated_text: Those who grasp at straws—the proponents of external objects (<s>bāhyārthavādins</s>) say:

body.text:
kiñca kriyādipratibhāsivijñānāt kāryaliṅgājjātaṃ yatparacittajñānaṃ
tatparacittaṃ viṣayīkriyata āhosvinna? viṣayīkaraṇe 'rthāntaraṃ syāt /
aviṣayatve tu kathaṃ jñānena paracittasattā pratīyate? tatsvarūpājñāne
tatsiddherasambhavāditi cet?
body.translated_text: Moreover, the cognition of other minds (<s>paracittajñāna</s>) that arises from the inferential mark of effect (<s>kāryaliṅga</s>)—namely, the cognition in which actions and so forth appear—does it take the other mind as its object, or does it not? If it takes it as object, it would become something different [i.e., direct perception]. But if it does not take it as object, then how is the existence of other minds cognized through that cognition? Since in the absence of knowledge of its true nature, the establishment thereof is impossible—if so objected?

body.text: kiñca kriyādipratibhāsītyādi / kriyādipratibhāso 'sti yasya vijñānasya tat kriyādipratibhāsivijñānam / tadeva kāryaliṅgam / tasmājjātaṃ kriyādipratibhāsivijñānāt kāryaliṅgājjātaṃ yat paracittasya svarūpaṃ viṣayīkaroti āhosvinneti dvidhā parīkṣā / prathamavikalpe doṣaṃ darśayotumāha - viṣayīkaraṇa ityādi / yadi nāma viṣayīkaroti, tadā tasya viṣayaḥ pṛthak syāt / dvitīyavikalpamupadarśayannāha - aviṣayatve tvityādi / atha na viṣayīkaroti, tadā kathaṃ paracittasattā jñāyate? kathaṃ na jñāyate? āha - tatsvarūpājñāna ityādi / tatsvarūpajñānādhīno hi bhāvopacāraḥ / sa tu tadabhāve na bhavatīti pūrvapakṣaḥ // 65 //
body.translated_text: 'Moreover, the cognition in which actions and so forth appear' and so forth. That cognition in which actions and so forth appear is the 'cognition in which actions and so forth appear.' That itself is the inferential mark of effect. From that arises—'from the cognition in which actions and so forth appear, from the inferential mark of effect, arises'—that which is knowledge of other minds: does it take the true nature of the other mind as its object, or not?—this is the twofold examination. To show the fault in the first alternative, he says 'if it takes as object' and so forth. If indeed it takes as object, then its object would be something separate. Presenting the second alternative, he says 'but if it does not take as object' and so forth. If it does not take as object, then how is the existence of other minds known? How is it not known? He says: 'Since in the absence of knowledge of its true nature' and so forth. For the designation of existence depends on knowledge of its true nature. But that does not obtain in the absence thereof—this is the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (opponent's objection). [Verse 65]

children.translated_text: This consequence also applies equally [to you].

body.text: samatāṃ darśayitumāha -
body.translated_text: To show the equality, he says:

body.text: kriyāvāgbhyāṃ paracittapratipattimatāmapi tatsvarūpaviṣayīkaraṇe svacittajñānavattadākārasyāpi jñānaṃ prasajyeta / tadajñāne tu tena tatsvarūpasya grahaṇaṃ katham /
body.translated_text: Even for those who accept the cognition of other minds through action and speech—if the true nature [of other minds] is taken as object, there would follow knowledge even of its [specific] aspect, just as with knowledge of one's own mind. But if there is no knowledge of that, then how can there be apprehension of its true nature by that [cognition]?

body.text: kriyāvāgbhyāmityādi / kiñca yadā bāhyārthāvādibhiḥ kriyāvāgbhyāṃ liṅgābhyāṃ paracittaṃ jñāyate, tadā tasya paracittasya svarūpaṃ viṣayīkriyata āhosvinna? yadi nāma viṣayīkriyate, tadā paracittasyākāro 'pi jñāyeta / atha na viṣayīkriyate, tadā tena jñānena pratipattrā vā kathaṃ jñāyeta? // 67 //
body.translated_text: 'Through action and speech' and so forth. Moreover, when the proponents of external objects know other minds through the two inferential marks of action and speech, is the true nature of those other minds taken as object, or not? If indeed it is taken as object, then the aspect of the other mind too would be known. If it is not taken as object, then how would it be known by that cognition or by the cognizer? [Verse 67]

body.text: bāhyārthāvādināṃ matamāśaṅkitumāha -
body.translated_text: Raising the position of the proponents of external objects as an objection, he says:

body.text:
atha liṅgāt sāmānyādhigateḥ nākārasya pratītiriti cet?
atha liṅgāt sāmānyādhigate ityādi / yasmālliṅgaṃ sāmānyena vyāptam, na tu viśeṣeṇa /

children.text: tasmātsāmānyameva jñāyate, na viśeṣa iti pūrvapakṣāśaṅkā // 68 //
children.translated_text: Therefore only the general is known, not the particular—this is the objection of the prior position. [Verse 68]

body.translated_text: 'Since from the inferential mark there is apprehension of the general, there is no cognition of the [specific] aspect'—if so objected? 'Since from the inferential mark there is apprehension of the general' and so forth. Since the inferential mark is pervaded by the general, not by the particular.

body.text: siddhāntavādyāha -
body.translated_text: The <s>siddhāntavādin</s> (proponent of the established position) says:

body.text: kiñca tatsāmānyaṃ paracittamevānyadvā 'hosvidavācyam /
body.translated_text: Moreover, is that general the other mind itself, or something different, or is it indescribable?

body.text: kiñca tatsāmānyamityādi / kiñca tatsāmānyaṃ paracittameva vā, anyadvā, āhosvidavācyamiti tridhā parīkṣā // 69 //
body.translated_text: 'Moreover, is that general' and so forth. Moreover, is that general the other mind itself, or something different, or is it indescribable?—this is the threefold examination. [Verse 69]

body.text: vikalpadvayaṃ nirākartumāha -
body.translated_text: To refute the two alternatives, he says:

body.text: anyatvāvācyatvayorekatve tvanena tatsāmānyameva gṛhyeta, na paracittam /
body.translated_text: In the case of difference or indescribability, being one [with the general], only that general would be apprehended by this [cognition], not the other mind.

body.text: tatkathamanena tad gamyate /
body.translated_text: Then how is that [other mind] cognized by this?

body.text: anyatvāvācyayorekatva ityādi / anyatvapakṣe sāmānyameva gṛhyeta, na paracittam / tasmāt kathamanena jñānena tat paracittaṃ jñāyate? avācyatvapakṣe 'pi eṣa eva nayaḥ // 70 //
body.translated_text: 'In the case of difference or indescribability, being one' and so forth. In the case of the difference alternative, only the general would be apprehended, not the other mind. Therefore, how is that other mind known by this cognition? In the case of the indescribability alternative too, this same reasoning [applies]. [Verse 70]

body.text: abhedapakṣaṃ nirākartumāha -
body.translated_text: To refute the non-difference alternative, he says:

body.text: nāpi sāmānyaṃ paracittameva / tathā sati tadākārastāpi jñānaṃ prasajyeta ityuktam /
body.translated_text: Nor is the general the other mind itself. In that case, there would follow knowledge even of its [specific] aspect—as has been stated.

body.text: nāpi sāmānyaṃ paracittamevetyādi / nāpi sāmānyaṃ paracittasya svarūpam / kasmāt? āha - athā satītyādi / yadi paracittādananyasya sāmānyasya grahaṇamabhyupagamyate, tadā paracittākārasyāpi jñānaṃ prasajyeta ityuktaṃ prāk // 71 //
body.translated_text: 'Nor is the general the other mind itself' and so forth. Nor is the general the true nature of the other mind. Why? He says: 'in that case' and so forth. If the apprehension of the general that is non-different from the other mind is accepted, then there would follow knowledge even of the aspect of the other mind—as stated before. [Verse 71]

body.text: syādetat - tathāstu, ko doṣaḥ? ucyate -
body.translated_text: One might think: let it be so—what is the fault? [He] says:

body.text: na hyeṣā anumānaprakriyā / na hyeṣā anumānaprakriyeti // 72 //
body.translated_text: For this is not the procedure of inference. 'For this is not the procedure of inference.' [Verse 72]

body.text: tadeva vivṛṇoti -
body.translated_text: He elaborates on that very point:

body.text: na hyanumānamarthasvarūpasya grāhakam / pratyakṣavat pratibhāsāsaviśiṣṭatvādeḥ prasaṅgāt / na hyanumānamarthasvarūpasyetyādi / na hyanumānaṃ svalakṣaṇasya grāhakatveneṣyate / pratyakṣeti tu vaidharmyadṛṣṭāntaḥ / kathanna svalakṣaṇasya grāhakatveneṣyate cet? āha - pratibhāsāviśiṣṭatvādeḥ prasaṅgāditi / anumānasyāpi pratyakṣavat sphuṭābhatā syāt / ādirityanena pratyakṣodbhūtadharmiṇo atītādiviṣayasya cāgrāhakatvamapi prasajyeta // 73 //
body.translated_text: For inference is not the apprehender of the true nature of an object. Because there would follow the consequence of [its being] indistinguishable in appearance from direct perception, and so forth. 'For inference is not [the apprehender] of the true nature of an object' and so forth. For inference is not accepted as the apprehender of the particular characteristic (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>). 'Direct perception' is the dissimilar example (<s>vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta</s>). How is it not accepted as the apprehender of the particular characteristic? He says: 'because of the consequence of indistinguishability of appearance' and so forth. Inference too, like direct perception, would have vivid appearance. By the word 'and so forth,' there would also follow the consequence of not apprehending objects beyond the scope of perception, such as past objects and so forth. [Verse 73]

body.text: syādetat - pratibhāsāviśiṣṭatvābhyupagamyata eveti / āha -
body.translated_text: One might think: let the indistinguishability of appearance be accepted. He says:

body.text: tena nāsya prāmāṇyam /
body.translated_text: Then this [inference] would have no validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>).

body.text: tena nāsya prāmāṇyamiti / pratibhāsāviśiṣṭatvādāvabhyupagate sati anumānenārthasvarūpasya grahaṇam / tena bhavatu prāmāṇyamiti cet? naiṣa nyāyaḥ // 74 //
body.translated_text: 'Then this would have no validity.' If the indistinguishability of appearance and so forth is accepted, then inference would apprehend the true nature of the object. If one says 'therefore let it have validity'—this reasoning is not correct. [Verse 74]

body.text: yadi pramāṇasya svalakṣaṇagrahaṇanibandhanatvaṃ neṣyate, tatkathamasya pramāṇyamiti cedāha -
body.translated_text: If the validity of a means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) is not accepted as grounded in the apprehension of the particular characteristic, then how can it have validity?—if so objected, he says:

body.text: tatsvarūpāgrahe 'pyabhipretārthāvisaṃvādāt prāmāṇyam /
body.translated_text: Even without apprehension of its true nature, [inference] has validity because of non-deviation from the intended object.

body.text: tatsvarūpāgrahe 'pītyādi / na hyanumānena viṣayasvarūpasya grahaṇam, apitu abhipretārthāvisaṃvādakatvāt prāmāṇyamiṣyate / kvacit granthe 'tena nāsya prāmāṇyam' iti pāṭhaḥ / tatra tvevaṃ yojanīyam - yadā pratibhāsādayo 'bhinnāḥ, tadā pramāṇameva na taditi / yadi anumānena svalakṣaṇaṃ gṛhyeta, tarhi pramāṇameva neṣyate / katham? āha - tatsvarūpāgrahe 'pītyādi / svarūpasyāgrahe 'pyabhipretārthāvisaṃvāditvādasya prāmāṇyam, na tu svalakṣaṇagrahaṇāditi // 75 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'tatsvarūpāgrahe 'pi' and so forth. For inference does not grasp the intrinsic nature (<s>svarūpa</s>) of the object; rather, its validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>) is accepted because it does not contradict the intended purpose. In some manuscripts, the reading is 'tena nāsya prāmāṇyam.' In that case, the construal should be thus: when representations and so forth are undifferentiated, then it is simply not a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition). If inference were to grasp the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (particular), then it would not be accepted as a <s>pramāṇa</s> at all. How so? He says 'tatsvarūpāgrahe 'pi' and so forth: even without grasping the intrinsic nature, its validity consists in non-contradiction with the intended purpose, not in grasping the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s>. [Verse 75]

body.text: syādevam - svalakṣaṇasyāgrahaṇe 'pyaparāparānumānena paracittamanumīyate / kathaṃ tadgrahaṇaṃ nivāryate? ata āha -
body.translated_text: One might say: even without grasping the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s>, through successive inferences the other's mind is inferred. How can the grasping of that be prevented? Therefore he says —

body.text:
dhūmādiliṅgājjātamapi na vahnyādisvarūpaviṣayi, dṛṣṭenāviśeṣaprasaṅgāt,
anumānasyātītādau niḥsvabhāvatāyāṃ cāpravṛtteḥ, arthakriyāprasaṅgācca /
body.translated_text: Even [a cognition] arising from inferential signs such as smoke does not have the intrinsic nature of fire and so forth as its object, because there would be the undesirable consequence of no difference from perception; and because inference does not operate regarding the essencelessness of past [and future objects]; and because there would be the undesirable consequence of causal efficacy.

body.text: dhūmādiliṅgājjātamapītyādi / na hi dhūmādiliṅgājjātamanumānaṃ vahnyādeḥ svarūpasya grāhakatveneṣyate / katham? āha - dṛṣṭenāviśeṣaprasaṅgāditi / yadyanumānaṃ svalakṣaṇaviṣayaṃ gṛhṇīyāt, tadā pratyakṣeṇa tulyatvaṃ prasajyeta / nāpyanumānamatītānāgataviṣayi, vastunaḥ niḥsvabhāvatāviṣayi ca syāt / pratyakṣapratibhāsasyevānumānavikalpapratibhāsasyāpyarthakriyākāritvaṃ syāt // 76 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'dhūmādiliṅgāj jātam api' and so forth. Inference arising from inferential signs such as smoke is not accepted as grasping the intrinsic nature of fire and so forth. How so? He says: 'because there would be the undesirable consequence of no difference from perception.' If inference were to grasp the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (particular), then it would absurdly become identical with perception. Nor could inference have past and future objects as its domain, nor could it have essencelessness (<s>niḥsvabhāvatā</s>) of things as its domain. And causal efficacy would absurdly follow for the conceptual representation of inference, just as for the direct appearance in perception. [Verse 76]

body.text: syādetat - paracittānumāne tasyāvisaṃvāditvameva nāsti / ata āha -
body.translated_text: One might say: in the inference of other minds, there is simply no non-contradiction at all. Therefore he says —

body.text: paracittānumāne 'pyabhipretārthāvisaṃvādo 'styeva /
body.translated_text: Even in the inference of other minds, there is indeed non-contradiction with the intended purpose.

body.text: paracittānumāne 'pītyādi // 77 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'paracittānumāne 'pi' and so forth. [Verse 77]

body.text: avisaṃvāditvasyopapattiṃ darśayannāha -
body.translated_text: Showing the justification for non-contradiction, he says —

body.text: tatpravartanadvāreṇa prāṇyantarasattāṃ pratipadya punaḥ punarvyavahārapravṛttau tadādhipatyādāgatārthasya prāpteḥ /
body.translated_text: Through the medium of engaging with that [other being], having ascertained the existence of another being, one attains the purpose that has come about through the dominance of that [other being], through repeated engagement in practical activity.

body.text: tatpravartanadvāreṇa prāṇyantaramityādi / pravṛttivyāpārāt paracittasyānumānam / taddvāreṇa prāṇyantarasattāṃ pratipadya yadi punaḥ punarvyavahārapravṛttimabhilāṣavyāyāmānyatrānyatragamanādikāṃ kuryāt, tadā prāṇyantararādhipatyenāgato 'rthassaṃlāpādiḥ prāpyate / atha vā punaḥ punarvyavahārapravṛttimabhilāṣavyāyāmadeśāntaragamanādikāṃ kuryāt, tadā prāṇyantarādhipatyena agato 'rthaḥ saṃlāpāt / atha vā punaḥ punarvyahāre pravartanamiti saṃlāpādanu gṛhapraveśaḥ, tadanu āsanadānam, tadanu cānnapānadānam, tadanu ca śayyāsanaprajñapanam, pādaprakṣālanodakadānam, pādamardanamityādīni // 78 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'tatpravartanadvāreṇa prāṇyantaram' and so forth. The inference of the other's mind is from the activity of engagement. Through that medium, having ascertained the existence of another being, if one then repeatedly engages in practical activity — efforts of desire, exertion, going from one place to another, and so forth — then the purpose that has come about through the dominance of the other being, namely conversation and the like, is obtained. Or alternatively: if one repeatedly engages in practical activity — efforts of desire, exertion, going to another place, and so forth — then the purpose that has come about through the dominance of the other being is [obtained], from conversation. Or alternatively: repeated engagement in practical activity means: following conversation, entering the house; then offering a seat; then giving food and drink; then arranging bedding and seat; giving water for washing feet; foot-massage — and so forth. [Verse 78]

body.text: kiṃ punaruttaravyahārasādhanāya prāmāṇyamiṣyata iti cet? ata āha -
body.translated_text: If one asks whether validity is accepted for the sake of subsequent practical activity, therefore he says —

body.text: tanmātraphalacintakasya lokasya prāṇyantarānumāne pravṛtteśca /
body.translated_text: Because the world, which considers only that much as the result, engages in the inference of other beings.

body.text: tanmātraphalacintakasyetyādi / tanmātraṃ phalamiti tanmātraphalam / taditi śabdo 'rthakriyāyāṃ vartate / mātreti śabdaḥ māne / yo lokaḥ tanmātraphalaṃ cintayati saḥ tanmātraphalacintakaḥ pravṛttaḥ / evamuktaṃ bhavati - yo laukikaprāṇyantarasattāmanuminoti, saḥ prāṇyantaradhipatyādāgatām arthakriyāṃ prāpnoti / ceti śabdena tanmātraṃ lokasya pravṛttiphalamityartho 'vasīyate // 79 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'tanmātraphalacintakasya' and so forth. 'That much as the result' is 'tanmātraphala'; the word 'that' refers to causal efficacy; the word 'mere' is in the sense of measure. The world that considers that much as the result — that is 'tanmātraphalacintaka' (one who considers only that much as the result) — is engaged. Thus it has been said: whoever infers the existence of other beings in the ordinary way obtains the causal efficacy that has come about through the dominance of the other being. And by the word 'ca' (and), the meaning is established that just that much is the result of the world's engagement. [Verse 79]

body.text: kathametat? āha -
body.translated_text: How is this? He says —

body.text: uttarārthaviśeṣapratibhāsijñānānubhavodayamātreṇa puruṣasya nirākāṅkṣatvāt /
body.translated_text: Because the person becomes satisfied through the mere arising of the experience of a cognition manifesting a subsequent specific object.

body.text: uttarārthaviśeṣapratibhāsītyādi / uttārārthaviśeṣo dāhapākādiḥ / tathā pratibhāsituṃ śīlaṃ yasya jñānasya tattathā / tasyānubhavaḥ uttarārthaviśeṣapratibhāsijñānānubhavaḥ / tasyodaya eva udayamātram / nirākāṅkṣa ityākāṅkṣārahitaḥ / tasya bhāvaḥ tattvam / tasmāt nirākāṅkṣatvāt / evamuktaṃ bhavati - yadā puruṣasya vahnyupalabdheranu dāhādipratibhāsijñānānubhavodayaḥ, tadaivāyaṃ nirākāṅkṣo bhavati // 80 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'uttarārthaviśeṣapratibhāsijñānānubhava' and so forth. The subsequent specific object is burning, cooking, and so forth. That whose disposition is to manifest thus — that is the cognition. Its experience is the 'experience of the cognition manifesting the subsequent specific object.' The mere arising of that is 'the mere arising.' 'Satisfied' (<s>nirākāṅkṣa</s>) means devoid of expectation. Its state is its nature. Therefore, because of being satisfied. Thus it has been said: when, after the person's perception of fire, there arises the experience of a cognition manifesting burning and so forth, at that very point he becomes satisfied. [Verse 80]

body.text: bhavatu tanmātreṇaiva puruṣaḥ nirākāṅkṣaḥ, kintu kathaṃ tanmātreṇa pūrvajñānasya prāmāṇyamiti cet? āha -
body.translated_text: Granted, the person is satisfied by just that much; but how does just that much constitute the validity of the prior cognition? To this he says —

body.text: pūrvajñānena vyavahārasamāpteḥ kṛtārthatvaṃ pramāṇatvena siddhatvāt / pūrvajñānenetyādi / yasmād yathoktavidhinā pūrvajñānena vyavahāraparisamāptiḥ, tasmād arthakriyākāritvaṃ pramāṇatvena vyavasthāpyate // 81 //
body.translated_text: Because, through the prior cognition, the completion of practical activity constitutes the fulfillment of purpose, which is established as validity. [The verse says] 'pūrvajñānena' and so forth. Since through the prior cognition, in the manner described, there is the completion of practical activity, therefore causal efficacy is established as validity. [Verse 81]

body.text: atra paro vyabhicāraṃ darśayannāha -
body.translated_text: Here the opponent, showing deviation, says —

body.text: nanu svapne 'pi pūrvajñānāduttarārthapratibhāsijñānāputpadyate / na tanmātreṇa pūrvajñānasya prāmāṇyaṃ yujyate, tadānīṃ sarveṣāṃ jñānānāṃ bhrāntatvāt /
body.translated_text: Objection: Even in dreams, from a prior cognition a cognition manifesting a subsequent object arises. Validity of the prior cognition cannot reasonably be established by that alone, because at that time all cognitions are erroneous.

body.text: nanu svapne 'pītyādi / svapne 'pi pūrvajñānanimittakamuttarārthakriyāpratibhāsijñānam utpadyate / na tanmātreṇa pūrvajñānasya prāmāṇyaṃ yujyate / kathaṃ na yujyate? āha - tadānīṃ sarveṣāṃ jñānānāmityādi / svapne sarvāṇi jñānāni bhrāntānyeveti pūrvapakṣaḥ // 82 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'nanu svapne 'pi' and so forth. Even in dreams, a cognition manifesting subsequent causal efficacy arises, caused by a prior cognition. The validity of the prior cognition cannot reasonably be established by that alone. Why not? He says: 'because at that time all cognitions' and so forth. In dreams, all cognitions are simply erroneous — this is the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (opponent's objection). [Verse 82]

body.text: siddhāntavādyāha -
body.translated_text: The <s>siddhāntavādin</s> (proponent) says —

body.text: tatra vijñaptijñānaṃ na kadāciccittaspandanādhipatyena vinā udbhavatītyataḥ tābhyāṃ te anumīyete / bhrāntivaśāt kadācid vyavahite 'pyudeti, na tu tadādhipatyarahitatvam / viśeṣastvasti sākṣātparamparayā cetyuktam /
body.translated_text: Therein, cognition of <s>vijñapti</s> (representation) never arises without the dominance of mental impulse (<s>cittaspandana</s>); therefore, from those two, those [other minds] are inferred. Due to the power of delusion, it sometimes arises even from a remote [impulse], but it is never devoid of that dominance. However, there is a distinction between direct and indirect [causation] — as has been stated.

body.text: tatra vijñaptijñānamityādi / kriyāvāgākārakaṃ jñānaṃ spandanādhipatyena vinā nodbhavati / ityataḥ tābhyāṃ te anumīyete / viśeṣastvasyeṣaḥ - tato 'pio upaplutāvasthāyāṃ vyavahitādhipatyāt paramparayā udayaḥ, jāgradavasthāyāṃ tu avyahitatvena / sarvametad vivecitaṃ prāgeva // 83 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'tatra vijñaptijñānam' and so forth. Cognition having the form of actions and speech does not arise without the dominance of impulse. Therefore, from those two, those [other minds] are inferred. However, the distinction is this: even in the disturbed state, the arising is through the dominance of a remote [impulse], indirectly; whereas in the waking state, it is through a non-remote [impulse]. All of this has been explained already. [Verse 83]

body.text: evaṃ vijñaptijñānānāmubhayorapyavasthayoḥ spandanāyattatvaṃ sādhayitvā svapnāvasthāyāṃ vijñaptijñānād uttarakālabhāvijñānāni yathā spandanāyattāni bhavanti tathā pratipādayitumāha - tatra yathā pūrvavijñaptijñānānāṃ paramparayā spandanādhipatyādudayaḥ tathā taduttarāvasthābhāvināmapi /
body.translated_text: Having thus established the dependence of <s>vijñapti</s>-cognitions on impulse in both states, in order to show how cognitions arising subsequent to <s>vijñapti</s>-cognition in the dream state are also dependent on impulse, he says — Therein, just as the arising of the prior <s>vijñapti</s>-cognitions is from the dominance of impulse indirectly, so too is [the arising] of those occurring in the subsequent state.

body.text: tatra yathā pūrvavijñaptijñānānāmityādi / svapnāvasthāyāṃ yathā pūrvavijñaptijñānānāṃ paramparayā spandanadhīpatyādudayaḥ, tathā taduttarāvasthābhāvināmapi / tatra paramparā tvevam - jāgradavasthāyāṃ prathamaṃ tāvat paraspandanādhipatyād vijñaptijñāne, tābhyāṃ prāṇyantarasattāyā anumānam, prāṇyantarasattānumānāt praveśajñānam, tadanu abhivādananamaskārajñāne, tābhyāmapyanu saṃlāpāsanadānādijñānam, tathā ca paṭhanapāṭhanasvādhyāyādijñānāni, tatastāvat kālakrameṇa śayanajñānam, tataḥ nidrāmupaiti / nidrāpūrvabhāvanāvaśācca punarvijñaptijñānayorudayaḥ / tataḥ punaḥ prāṇyantarasattāyā anumānam / tataśca punaḥ praveśasaṃlāpādijñānānāmudayaḥ // 84 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'tatra yathā pūrvavijñaptijñānānām' and so forth. In the dream state, just as the arising of the prior <s>vijñapti</s>-cognitions is from the dominance of impulse indirectly, so too is [the arising] of those occurring in the subsequent state. The indirect chain is as follows: in the waking state, first, from the dominance of another's impulse, <s>vijñapti</s>-cognition [arises]; from those two, the inference of the existence of another being; from the inference of the existence of another being, cognition of entering; then cognitions of greeting and salutation; then from those, cognitions of conversation, offering a seat, and so forth; likewise, cognitions of reading, teaching, self-study, and so forth; then in due course of time, cognition of lying down; then one enters sleep. And through the force of the impressions (<s>bhāvanā</s>) preceding sleep, again the arising of <s>vijñapti</s>-cognitions. Then again, inference of the existence of another being. Then again, the arising of cognitions of entering, conversation, and so forth. [Verse 84]

body.text: praveśādijñānānāṃ pāramparyeṇotpattiḥ / tāmeva darśayannāha -
body.translated_text: The arising of cognitions of entering and so forth is through a chain. Showing that very chain, he says —

body.text: vijñaptijñānāśrayaspandanottarāvasthācittasantānādeva paramparayotpādaḥ /
body.translated_text: The arising is through a chain, from the mind-stream of the state subsequent to the impulse that is the basis of <s>vijñapti</s>-cognition.

body.text: vijñaptijñānāśrayetyādi / jāgradavasthāyāṃ vijñaptijñānasyāśrayo yatparasantānavartispandanaṃ tasya uttarāvasthā, yā pramātranumānasyottaravartisaṃlāpādivyavahārākārajñānajananasamarthā / tadbhāvīni yāni cittāni vijñaptijñānāśrayaspandanottarāvasthācittasantānaḥ, tasmād yathoktaprakāreṇa svapnāvasthāyāṃ praveśādijñānānāṃ paramparayotpādaḥ // 85 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'vijñaptijñānāśraya' and so forth. In the waking state, the impulse that is in another's mind-stream and that serves as the basis of <s>vijñapti</s>-cognition — the state subsequent to that, which is capable of generating cognitions in the form of practical activity such as conversation, which follow upon the inferring subject's inference. The mental moments that belong to that state are the 'mind-stream of the state subsequent to the impulse that is the basis of <s>vijñapti</s>-cognition'; from that, in the manner described, the arising of cognitions of entering and so forth in the dream state is through a chain. [Verse 85]

body.text: syānmatam - bhavatu paramparayotpādaḥ, vyabhicārastu tadavastha eva / ata evāha -
body.translated_text: One might think: granted, the arising is through a chain, but the deviation applies in that very state. Therefore he says —

body.text: tatrāpi yādṛganumānaṃ tādṛgavisaṃvādo vyavahāraścāpyastyeveti kenāpi na gṛhyete /
body.translated_text: Even therein, there is non-contradiction and practical activity of the same kind as the inference — this is not grasped by anyone [as contradictory].

body.text: tatrā yādṛganumānamityādi / svapnāvasthāyāmapi yādṛk yāvatkālaṃ paracittasya anumānaṃ tādṛk tāvatkālamātraṃ saṃlāpādirūpo 'visaṃvādo 'styeva / anyo 'nyasaṃbaddho vyavahāraścāpi tāvatkālamrātramastyeva / ityataḥ na kaścid vyabhicāradoṣaḥ / anyaiścāsyaivānyathā vyākhyā kriyate / ta evaṃ vyācakṣate - tatra svapnāvasthāyāmapi kāryaliṅgasya kāraṇe 'vyabhicārād yādṛk utpattidharmatayā paramparayā pūrvajñānasyānumānam, tādṛk aprabuddhacittasyāpyarthakriyāpratibhāsodayalakṣaṇo 'visaṃvādo 'styeva / kālaviprakṛṣṭākārānumānasyāvisaṃvādalakṣaṇasadbhāvādeva vyavahāraścāpi / ityataḥ kenāpi na gṛhyata iti // 86 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'tatra yādṛk anumānam' and so forth. Even in the dream state, just as and for just as long as there is inference of the other mind, so and for just that long there is non-deception in the form of conversation and such. And mutual conventional dealings also exist for just that duration. Therefore there is no fault of deviation. Others give a different interpretation of this very [verse]. They explain it thus: In the dream state too, since the inferential mark of effect does not deviate from the cause, just as there is inference of the prior cognition through the nature of origination in succession, so too even for the mind of one who is not awakened, there is non-deception characterized by the arising of manifestation of purposeful activity. And conventional dealings also exist precisely because of the existence of non-deception characterized by temporally distant inference. Therefore this is not grasped [as a fault] by anyone. [Verse 86]

body.text: tathā parābhūto 'pi bāhyārthavādī dhṛtimatyajan punarācaṣṭe -
body.translated_text: Thus, even though defeated, the <s>bāhyārthavādin</s> (external realist), not abandoning his firmness, speaks again —

body.text: paracittānumānena tatsvarūpāgrahe 'pyavisaṃvādād bhavatu tathā prāmāṇyam /
body.translated_text: Through inference of other minds, even though the intrinsic nature of the other mind is not grasped, let there be validity due to non-deception.

body.text: sākṣāt paracittavidāṃ tu katham? yadi tāvat paracittasya svarūpaṃ sākṣāt jānanti, tadā tasyārthāntaragrahaṇaṃ syāt / atha na jānanti, kathaṃ te sākṣādvidaḥ?
body.translated_text: But what about those who directly know other minds? If they know the intrinsic nature of the other mind directly, then their cognition would grasp an entirely different object. But if they do not know it, how are they 'direct knowers'?

body.text: paracittānumānenetyādi / paracittānumānena tatsvarūpāgrahe 'pyavisaṃvādād bhavatu tasya prāmāṇyam, ye tu sākṣāt paracittavidaḥ teṣāṃ tu katham? yadi tāvat paracittasya svarūpaṃ sākṣājjānanti, tadāsya pratyakṣasya grāhyamarthāntaraṃ syāt / atha na jānanti, tadā kathaṃ te yoginaḥ sākṣādvida iti matam // 87 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'paracittānumānena' and so forth. Through inference of other minds, even though the intrinsic nature is not grasped, let there be validity due to non-deception. But what about those who are direct knowers of other minds? If they know the intrinsic nature of the other mind directly, then the object of this direct perception would be an entirely different thing. But if they do not know it, then how are those <s>yogins</s> direct knowers? — this is the view. [Verse 87]

body.text: hetumupasaṃharannāha -
body.translated_text: Applying the reason, he says —

body.text: kathaṃ nāma pratyakṣeṇārthasvarūpasyāgrahaṇaṃ ca bhavati / atha na gṛhyate, kathaṃ tarhi pramaṇamiti cet?
body.translated_text: How is it possible that there is no grasping of the intrinsic nature of an object by direct perception? But if it is not grasped, how then is it a valid means of knowledge?

body.text: kathaṃ nāma pratyakṣeṇetyādi / pratyakṣamarthasvarūpasya grāhakamitīṣyate / yadi arthasvarūpaṃ na gṛhyate, kīdṛk tatpratyakṣam? arthasvarūpāgrahaṇe pramāṇatvaṃ nirākartumāha - atha na gṛhyate kathaṃ tarhi pramāṇamiti / svarūpagrahaṇanibandhanaṃ hyasya pramāṇatvam / iti pūrvapakṣāśaṅkā // 88 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'kathaṃ nāma pratyakṣeṇa' and so forth. Direct perception is accepted as the grasper of the intrinsic nature of an object. If the intrinsic nature of the object is not grasped, what kind of direct perception is that? To refute its status as a valid means of knowledge in the absence of grasping the intrinsic nature, he says: 'But if it is not grasped, how then is it a valid means of knowledge?' For its status as a valid means of knowledge depends on grasping the intrinsic nature — this is the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (opponent's objection). [Verse 88]

body.text: siddhāntavādinaḥ -
body.translated_text: [The view] of the <s>siddhāntavādin</s> (proponent) —

body.text: aprahīṇagrāhyagrāhakavikalpayogināṃ paracittajñānamapi vyavahāre 'visaṃvādādeva pramāṇam, rūpādidarśanavat; āśrayāparāvṛtteḥ /
body.translated_text: For <s>yogins</s> who have not abandoned the conceptualization of subject and object, even their cognition of other minds is a valid means of knowledge in conventional dealings precisely due to non-deception, just like the perception of forms and such; because their basis has not been transformed.

body.text: aprahīṇagrāhyagrāhakavikalpayogināmityādi / aprahīṇaḥ grāhyagrāhakavikalpo yeṣāṃ yogināṃ teṣāṃ tathā / teṣāṃ yat paracittajñānaṃ tad vyavahāre 'visaṃvādādeva pramāṇam, asmadādisambaddharūpādidarśanavat / na tu svarūpagrahaṇāt / aprahīṇagrāhyagrāhakavikalpasya hetum āha - āśrayāparāvṛtteriti / tathā hi, teṣāmālayavijñānalakṣaṇamaparāvṛttam / tasya parāvṛttiḥ grāhyagrāhakavikalpavāsanāyāḥ prahāṇam // 89 //
body.translated_text: [The verse says] 'aprahīṇagrāhyagrāhakavikalpayoginām' and so forth. Those <s>yogins</s> for whom the conceptualization of apprehended and apprehender has not been abandoned — they are so described. Their cognition of other minds is a valid means of knowledge in conventional dealings precisely due to non-deception, just like the perception of forms and such connected with us ordinary beings. But not due to grasping the intrinsic nature. He states the reason for the non-abandonment of subject-object conceptualization: 'because the basis has not been transformed.' Indeed, their <s>ālayavijñāna</s> (storehouse consciousness) — their basis — has not been transformed. The transformation of that basis is the abandonment of the latent impressions of subject-object conceptualization. [Verse 89]

body.text: yadi paracittajñānaṃ na svarūpasya grāhakam, kathaṃ tarhi tat sphuṭākārakaṃ bhavatīti cet? āha -
body.translated_text: If the cognition of other minds does not grasp the intrinsic nature, how then does it arise with a vivid appearance? He says —

body.text: yogabalāddhi teṣāṃ jñānaṃ paracittakāraviśeṣānukāri sphuṭābhamupajāyate, karmadevādyadhiṣṭhānabalāt satyasvapnadarśanavat / yogabalāddhītyādi / bhāvanābalāddhi yogināṃ paracittajñānaṃ paracittākāraviśeṣānukāri sphuṭamupajāyate, yathā karmabalād devādyadhiṣṭhānabalācca satyasvapnadarśināṃ jñānaṃ sphuṭamarthākāramudeti // 90 //
body.translated_text: Through the power of <s>yoga</s>, their cognition arises as a vivid appearance that mirrors the specific forms of the other mind, just as the vision of true dreams arises through the power of <s>karma</s> and the empowerment of gods and such. [The verse says] 'yogabalāt' and so forth. Through the power of meditation, the <s>yogins'</s> cognition of other minds arises as a vivid one that mirrors the specific forms of the other mind, just as the cognition of those who have true dream visions arises with a vivid form of the object through the power of <s>karma</s> and through the power of empowerment by gods and such. [Verse 90]

body.text: yadyevaṃ cintyeta - bhavatu bhāvanābalādeva yogināṃ paracittajñānam, tena cittasvarūpasyāgrahaṇaṃ tu kathamiti / āha -
body.translated_text: If one were to consider thus: granted, the <s>yogins'</s> cognition of other minds is produced by the power of meditation alone, but how then does it not grasp the intrinsic nature of the mind? He says —

body.text: teṣāmapi na paracittāviṣayitvena jñānamudeti / te 'pi tadākārasadṛśasvacittapratibhāsameva jānantītyevamavadhāraṇād paracittavida iti vyavahāraḥ / teṣāmapi na paracittaviṣayitvenetyādi / tat bhāvanābalājjātamapi paracittasya svarūpaṃ viṣayīkartuṃ na samartham / tathāvidhānāṃ yogināṃ grāhyagrāhakaviklpasyāprahīṇatvāt / yadi yoginaḥ paracittasya svarūpaṃ na jānanti, kathaṃ paracittavida ityavadhāryate cet? āha - te 'pi svacittapratibhāsam ityādi / yogino 'pi paracittākārasadṛśena svacittapratibhāsenaiva paracittaṃ jānanti [iti paracittavidaḥ] ityevamavadhāraṇaṃ kṛtvā vyavahāraḥ pravartate // 91 //
body.translated_text: Even their cognition does not arise as having the other mind for its direct object. They too know only the manifestation of their own mind resembling the form of the other mind — and it is through such a conventional determination that the term 'knower of other minds' is used. [The verse says] 'teṣām api na paracittaviṣayitvena' and so forth. Even that cognition born of the power of meditation is not capable of making the intrinsic nature of the other mind its direct object, because for <s>yogins</s> of that kind, the conceptualization of apprehended and apprehender has not been abandoned. If the <s>yogins</s> do not know the intrinsic nature of the other mind, how is the determination 'knower of other minds' made? He says: 'They too know through the manifestation of their own mind' and so forth. <s>Yogins</s> too know the other mind only through the manifestation of their own mind resembling the form of the other mind — having made the determination that they are 'knowers of other minds' in this way, conventional usage proceeds. [Verse 91]

body.text: yadi tat svarūpaṃ na gṛhṇāti, kathaṃ tarhi pratyakṣam? kathaṃ ca prāmāṇyamiti cedāha -
body.translated_text: If it does not grasp the intrinsic nature, how then is it direct perception? And how is it a valid means of knowledge? He says —

body.text: tadākārānukārisphuṭābhatvāt tatpratyakṣam, avisaṃvāaditvācca prāmāṇamiti matam / tadākārānukārisphuṭābhatvāt tatpratyakṣamityādi / yasmāt paracittasyākāraṃ sphuṭamanukaroti, tasmāt pratyakṣamiti matam / yasmāccāvisaṃvādi tasmāt pramāṇam // 92 //
body.translated_text: Because it has a vivid appearance that mirrors the forms of the other mind, it is 'direct perception' of that [mind]; and because it is non-deceptive, it is a valid means of knowledge — this is the view. [The verse says] 'tadākārānukārisphuṭābhatvāt tatpratyakṣam' and so forth. Since it vividly mirrors the form of the other mind, therefore it is held to be direct perception. And since it is non-deceptive, therefore it is a valid means of knowledge. [Verse 92]

body.text: prahīṇagrāhyagrāhakavikalpānāṃ tathāgatānāṃ yat paracittajñānam, tat paracittasya svarūpaṃ viṣayīkaroti, āhosvinna / yadi karoti, tasyārtho 'rthāntaraṃ syāt / atha na karoti, tadā bhagavataḥ jñānamapyayathārtha syāditi cet? āha -
body.translated_text: Regarding the cognition of other minds possessed by <s>Tathāgatas</s> who have abandoned the conceptualization of subject and object: does it make the intrinsic nature of the other mind its direct object, or does it not? If it does, its object would be an entirely different thing. But if it does not, then even the <s>Bhagavān's</s> cognition would be inaccurate? He says —

body.text: acintyo hi bhagavataḥ sarvārthādhigamaḥ, sarvathā jñānabhidhānaviṣayātītatvāt / acintyo hi bhagavataḥ sarvārthādhigama ityādi / acintyo hi yogivaryāṇāṃ tathā gatānāṃ buddhagocaraḥ / teṣāṃ tu na kevalaṃ paracittajñānamacintyam, api tvaviśeṣeṇa sarvārthasarvākārajñānamapi acintyam / kasmāt? āha - tadavasthāyāḥ sarvathā jñānabhidhānaviṣayātītatvāditi /
body.translated_text: Inconceivable indeed is the <s>Bhagavān's</s> realization of all objects, because it utterly transcends the domain of cognition and expression. [The verse says] 'acintyo hi bhagavataḥ sarvārthādhigamaḥ' and so forth. Inconceivable indeed is the domain of the <s>Tathāgatas</s>, the supreme among <s>yogins</s>. For them, not only is the cognition of other minds inconceivable, but without exception, their knowledge of all objects in all aspects is also inconceivable. Why? He says: because that state utterly transcends the domain of cognition and expression.

body.text: tathāgataḥ jñānādanyajñānenāvadhārayitumaśakyatvāt jñānaviṣayātītaḥ / tasmād svarūpasya yathāvadanadhigamādeva abhidhānaviṣayātītaḥ /
body.translated_text: The <s>Tathāgata</s> transcends the domain of cognition because he cannot be comprehended by any cognition other than his own. Therefore, precisely because the intrinsic nature is not realized as it truly is [by ordinary cognition], he transcends the domain of expression.

body.text: tathāgatānāṃ punaḥ dvividhaṃ sarvārthajñānam / ādarśajñānena sarvadharmasvabhāvatathatājñānam, pratyavekṣaṇajñānena ca sarvavastujñānam / tatra ādarśajñānaṃ grāhyagrāhakavikalpenāsamprayuktaṃ bhavati / sarvadharmasvabhāvatathatāyāḥ vedanāt sarvārthajñānam, lokottarajñānasvabhāvatvāt / pratyavekṣaṇajñānaṃ lokottarajñānapṛṣṭhalabdhagrāhyagrāhakavikalpasaṃprayuktāt sarvasūkṣmāvṛtavyavahitavastūnāṃ sarvākāraṃ jānātītyataḥ laukikasarvākārajñānam, lokottarajñānapṛṣṭhalabdhalaukikajñānasvabhāvatvāt / tasmāt pratyavekṣaṇajñānaṃ sarvārthajñānanayena na virudhyate / nāpi vitatham, tasya grāhyagrāhakavikalpasadbhāvābhyupagamāt, tasya cāvitathatvena darśanāt /
body.translated_text: The <s>Tathāgatas</s>, furthermore, have twofold knowledge of all objects. Through <s>ādarśajñāna</s> (mirror-like wisdom), they have knowledge of the <s>tathatā</s> (suchness) — the intrinsic nature of all <s>dharmas</s>. Through <s>pratyavekṣaṇajñāna</s> (discriminating wisdom), they have knowledge of all things. Of these, <s>ādarśajñāna</s> is unconditioned by the conceptualization of apprehended and apprehender. It is knowledge of all objects through the realization of the <s>tathatā</s> — the intrinsic nature of all <s>dharmas</s> — because it has the nature of supramundane wisdom. <s>Pratyavekṣaṇajñāna</s>, being associated with the conceptualization of apprehended and apprehender obtained subsequent to supramundane wisdom, knows all aspects of all subtle, hidden, and obstructed things — therefore it is mundane knowledge of all aspects, because it has the nature of mundane wisdom obtained subsequent to supramundane wisdom. Therefore <s>pratyavekṣaṇajñāna</s> is not contradicted by the principle of omniscience. Nor is it erroneous, because the existence of subject-object conceptualization in it is accepted, and it is seen to be non-erroneous.

body.text: samatājñānamādarśajñānamālambate,pratītyasamutpannavastumātraviṣayitvāt / kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñānaṃ tu svasāmānyalakṣaṇaviṣayi / evaṃ sati caturjñānasvabhāvaḥ tathāgataḥ / tatra ādarśajñānaṃ lokottaram / tatpṛṣṭhalabdhānyanyāni ca laukikāni / tadevaṃ bhagavataḥ sarvārthajñānam eteṣu caturṣu yathāyogaṃ yojanīyam // 93 //
body.translated_text: <s>Samatājñāna</s> (wisdom of equality) takes <s>ādarśajñāna</s> as its basis, because it has as its object merely things arisen through dependent origination. <s>Kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna</s> (wisdom of accomplishing activities), however, has both particular and general characteristics as its object. This being so, the <s>Tathāgata</s> has the nature of four wisdoms. Of these, <s>ādarśajñāna</s> is supramundane. The others, obtained subsequent to it, are mundane. Thus the <s>Bhagavān's</s> omniscience should be connected as appropriate with these four [wisdoms]. [Verse 93]

children.translated_text: From the commentary on the <s>Saṃtānāntarasiddhi</s> (Proof of Other Mind-Streams), through the explanation with word-analysis,
whatever merit I have obtained — through that, may beings attain realization.
